rows.title: 1675 Mercock Land Dispute
rows.summary: A 1675 record preserves Tackapousha challenging colonial possession of "Mercock" land, stating that the land Hempstead enjoyed had not been paid for. The statement places Merrick/Mercock land within ongoing disputes over payment, authority, and colonial occupation. Tackapousha's challenge shows Native diplomacy and legal resistance rather than land loss as inevitable or uncontested.
rows.address_label: Merrick / Hempstead south shore land dispute landscape
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land through the Mercock/Merrick land reference and south shore Hempstead context.
rows.why_this_matters: The 1675 Mercock dispute shows that Native leaders challenged colonial land claims and named unpaid land as an injustice. Dispossession appears here as a contested process involving diplomacy, law, pressure, and resistance.

rows.title: Accabonac
rows.summary: Accabonac is a placename in East Hampton associated with Accabonac Harbor, Springs, and nearby meadows adjoining Gardiner's Bay. Recorded forms include Acabonack and Acabonuk, and early records often apply the name to the meadows.
rows.address_label: Accabonac Harbor / Springs, East Hampton, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Accabonac preserves an Indigenous geographic description of East Hampton's estuarine landscape, with records connecting the name to a place where edible ground-nuts grow. Its many recorded spellings show how Native language, local ecology, and colonial paperwork intersect, often imperfectly, in the written record. The name keeps Long Island visible as a Native homeland shaped by land, water, plant knowledge, and continuing community memory.

rows.title: Acombamack
rows.summary: Acombamack is a Long Island Algonquian placename associated with the neck of land where Bellport is now located in Brookhaven. The place is described in relation to Great South Bay and the land between Daytons Brook and Overtons Brook, with Owenamchock treated as a related boundary and fishing-place form.
rows.address_label: General Bellport / Great South Bay area, Brookhaven, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Acombamack preserves a Native placename for the Bellport area along Great South Bay, where records associate the name with a fishing place. Its many colonial-era spellings show how Indigenous geography entered English paperwork imperfectly, but still carried knowledge of water, foodways, and local movement. The South Shore was and remains more than a modern shoreline; it is part of Native coastal geography.

rows.title: Amagansett Indian Well
rows.summary: Amagansett Indian Well is connected with the Amagansett placename and the Indian Well plain in East Hampton.
rows.address_label: Amagansett Indian Well / Indian Well Beach area, East Hampton, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Amagansett Indian Well connects a familiar East Hampton placename to Native knowledge of water, fishing places, and coastal life on the East End. The recorded spellings show how a Native name moved through colonial documents while still preserving a relationship between people, plain, well, and shore. Everyday place names can carry Indigenous geography and memory into the present.

rows.title: Anchannock
rows.summary: Anchannock is Tooker's recorded Indigenous name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay. The name is interpreted as land well wooded or full of timber.
rows.address_label: Robins Island, Peconic Bay, Southold, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Anchannock preserves an Indigenous name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay, with an interpretation tied to land that was well wooded or full of timber. That meaning points to the practical ways Native place names can describe ecology, resources, and how people understood island landscapes. Read beside the modern English name, Anchannock keeps older layers of Peconic Bay language and memory present.

rows.title: Anendesak / Eaton's Neck
rows.summary: A Huntington-area tract name tied to Eaton's Neck, Eader Necks Beach, and the Assawanama/Fresh Pond boundary landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Anendesak matters even though its exact meaning has not been identified, because the recorded name preserves a Native layer of Huntington-area geography beneath the later English name Eaton's Neck. Its survival in written records shows how Indigenous place knowledge can remain visible even when translation is uncertain. The name keeps attention on a North Shore neck of land that carried Native meaning before later colonial ownership names took over.

rows.title: Anock
rows.summary: Anock is an Indigenous place name connected with a short creek at the bottom of Fourth Neck in the East Quogue area of Southampton, historically called Atlanticville. It is close to, but distinct from, the nearby Weesuck place name.
rows.address_label: General southern Fourth Neck / East Quogue creek area, Southampton, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Anock preserves a Native creek name in the East Quogue area, even though no settled translation has been found. Its short form shows how Indigenous names could be compressed or altered in English records while still pointing to specific waterways and necks of land. The South Fork landscape was shaped by Native language, movement, and memory before later town and property names took hold.

rows.title: Anuskkummikak
rows.summary: Anuskkummikak is an Indigenous place name connected with the upland part of Little East Neck in Babylon, formerly also called Captain Fleet's Neck. The surviving description places the name on the upland planting ground rather than the creek or meadow.
rows.address_label: General upland Little East Neck / Babylon area, Babylon, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Anuskkummikak preserves a Native description of Little East Neck as planting land, linking the Babylon shoreline to foodways, seasonal work, and careful land use. Its variant spellings show how a Native agricultural term was carried into colonial records through imperfect English writing. Fields, necks, and waterways were part of connected community landscapes across Indigenous Long Island.

rows.title: Apocock
rows.summary: A Westhampton meadow-and-upland name related linguistically to Appaquogue, with forms including Apaucuck, Appocock, and Apockac.
rows.address_label: Beaverdam Creek, Westhampton, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Apocock connects the Beaverdam Creek area to wetland plants, meadowland, and the practical materials of Native coastal life. Its interpretation as flaggy land or a covering-place points to reeds and other plants used for mats, shelters, and everyday work, while related records also place the creek within a broader Native territorial landscape. Wetlands were knowledgeable homelands shaped by language, ecology, and community use, not empty margins.

rows.title: Appaquogue
rows.summary: Appaquogue, also written Apoquogue, is identified as an East Hampton placename for a farming district near a flaggy meadow. The same source notes that the vicinity was locally called Lily Pond. It is kept separate from Apocock in Westhampton because the sources describe different places, even though the names share a related meaning.
rows.address_label: Lily Pond, East Hampton, NY (approximate)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Appaquogue preserves an East Hampton placename tied to a flaggy meadow near the Lily Pond area, where useful wetland plants were part of the local landscape. Its interpretation as a place where flags grow points to Native ecological knowledge and to materials used in mats, coverings, and everyday life. The name links language, plants, water, and community use in one remembered place.

rows.title: Appopottamax
rows.summary: Appopottamax is recorded as the name of a creek at Bay Shore, mentioned in a Brooklyn Times notice from January 26, 1899. The source also cautions that the name was not otherwise on record and that no other authority had been found for it.
rows.address_label: Bay Shore, NY (specific creek unidentified)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Appopottamax matters partly because it is uncertain: the name is recorded from a single later newspaper notice, with a suggested meaning connected to a fishing place by a brook. That caution shows how Native placenames can survive unevenly in print, sometimes as fragments that need careful reading rather than overconfidence. Even so, the Bay Shore creek setting points to a broader South Shore geography of fishing, waterways, and Indigenous place memory.

rows.title: Aquebogue
rows.summary: Aquebogue is a major Riverhead-area placename for land on the north side of the Peconic River and Peconic Bay. Recorded spellings and related forms include Ucquebaug, Occabauk, Occabock, Occobauk, Agabake, Ocquebauk, Ahkobauk, Ackqueboug, Aucquobouke, Occapogue, Aukabog, Pahehetock, and the transcription error Omkalog.
rows.address_label: Aquebogue, Riverhead, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Aquebogue preserves a Native placename for the Peconic River and Bay landscape in Riverhead, with one interpretation connecting it to the head of the bay. Its many recorded spellings show how English documents tried to capture an Indigenous name tied to water, direction, and local geography. The Peconic region appears here as a Native waterway system where names carried practical knowledge of bays, rivers, travel, and homelands.

rows.title: Araca
rows.summary: Araca is a south-shore West Neck placename in present-day Amityville, Babylon. It is recorded in a 1697 deed and interpreted as beyond, furthermost, or further, describing its position as the westernmost neck of the old Huntington bounds.
rows.address_label: West Neck, Amityville, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Araca preserves a Native directional name from a 1697 deed for the West Neck area of present-day Amityville, with meanings such as beyond or furthermost. That kind of placename shows how people described land in relation to movement, shorelines, and neighboring places rather than only by fixed modern boundaries. The South Shore is a layered geography where colonial deed language still carries traces of Indigenous spatial knowledge.

rows.title: Arasecoseagge
rows.summary: Arasecoseagge is recorded as a Babylon placename for the easternmost East Neck, also known in English as Captain Fleet's Neck. The name designated the meadow portion of the neck, while Anuskkummikak referred to the upland.
rows.address_label: Argyle Park / Captain Fleet's Neck area, Babylon, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Arasecoseagge preserves a Native name for the meadow portion of Captain Fleet's Neck, interpreted as the furthermost meadow. The name distinguishes wet meadowland from nearby upland and shows how local geography could be described with ecological precision. A colonial deed reference becomes evidence of Native land knowledge, where meadows, necks, and shorelines were part of an understood South Shore landscape.

rows.title: Areshunk
rows.summary: Areshunk is a Center Moriches placename for a neck of land and landing near the foot of Union Avenue. The name appears to preserve a corrupted form of Warishone, the name of an Unkechaug man associated with the neck.
rows.address_label: Foot of Union Avenue, Center Moriches, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Areshunk preserves a Center Moriches neck-and-landing name that records suggest may be connected to Warishone or Worishun, a Native personal or local name in the written record. That possibility matters because place names can preserve not only landforms, but also remembered people, families, and community presence. Even imperfect colonial records can point back to Native lives and relationships with specific shorelines.

rows.title: Arhakaamunk
rows.summary: Arhakaamunk connects Crab Meadow in Huntington with Native place naming, coastal foodways, and the difficulty of reading variant colonial spellings.
rows.address_label: Crab Meadow, Huntington, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Arhakaamunk preserves a Native name for the Crab Meadow area of Huntington, with related forms that show how difficult these names were for English recorders to spell consistently. Interpretive context connects the name to crab fishing and coastal resources, making it a reminder that marine life shaped local knowledge and place memory. Foodways, water, and language meet here in a North Shore coastal landscape.

rows.title: Asawsunce
rows.summary: A Brookhaven wetland placename where a Native personal name appears to remain attached to swamp and Yaphank Creek geography.
rows.address_label: Yaphank Creek wetlands south of Yaphank, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Asawsunce appears to preserve a Native personal name connected with a swamp and Yaphank Creek locality in Brookhaven. Instead of only describing a landform, the name points toward a person or family remembered through place, showing how Native lives could become embedded in local geography. Wetlands and creek names can hold community memory, not empty space on a map.

rows.title: Ashawagh
rows.summary: Ashawagh is a Montaukett placename and settlement locality at Hand's Creek, near Three Mile Harbor in East Hampton. It as a locality where shell heaps, arrow points, and pottery fragments marked an Indigenous village site. The name is interpreted as a place between, referring to land between the creek branches.
rows.address_label: Hand's Creek / Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Ashawagh preserves a Montaukett placename for a settlement locality at Hand's Creek near Three Mile Harbor, interpreted as a place between or in the middle. That meaning fits a creek-and-harbor landscape where position, water access, fishing, shellfish, and travel all mattered. East Hampton's waterways remain part of continuing Montaukett geography and memory, not only scenic views or modern place names.

rows.title: Aspatuck Creek
rows.summary: A western Southampton creek name connected with Ketchaponack Neck, Quiogue, and older spellings including Aspatatuck and Assopatuck.
rows.address_label: Aspatuck Creek near Westhampton and Quiogue, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Aspatuck Creek preserves a Native waterway name in western Southampton between Ketchaponack Neck and Quiogue, even though no settled translation has been found. Its recorded forms show how English documents tried to represent a local name tied to creek, neck, and bay geography. Even uncertain placenames can mark real Indigenous relationships with waterways that shaped travel, foodways, and community memory.

rows.title: Assasquage
rows.summary: Assasquage is identified with Great Meadow Creek near Jamesport in Riverhead town. The name appears in a 1648 deed for the tract commonly called Ocquebauck, where planting land was reserved between Miamegg and Assasquage. The name is interpreted as a great grass place or great marshy place.
rows.address_label: Great Meadow Creek / South Jamesport area, Riverhead, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Assasquage preserves a Native name for Great Meadow Creek near Jamesport, interpreted as a great grass place or great meadow. The 1648 deed context connects the creek to nearby planting land, showing how waterways, meadow ecology, and cultivation were recorded together in colonial paperwork. Riverhead's creeks and meadows belong to Indigenous land relationships and foodways, not just background scenery.

rows.title: Assawanama
rows.summary: A Fresh Pond place name at Fort Salonga, connected with Huntington-Smithtown boundary history and several related recorded forms.
rows.address_label: Fresh Pond, Fort Salonga, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Assawanama preserves a Fresh Pond placename at Fort Salonga, where the name includes several related, disputed, or overlapping forms. Interpretive context connects the name with fishing-place meanings, while the variant spellings show how complex Native geography could become tangled in colonial documentation. Careful history sometimes means holding uncertainty while still recognizing water, fish, and local knowledge as central to Indigenous Long Island.

rows.title: Assups Neck
rows.summary: Assups is recorded as a name applied to two necks of land in western Southampton town. The history represents the primary Assups Neck east of Quantuck Creek. The other form, Little Assups, belongs with the later Quiogue entry.
rows.address_label: Neck east of Quantuck Creek, Quogue/Quiogue area, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Assups Neck may preserve a Native personal name attached to a Southampton neck of land east of Quiogue. If the name comes from Assup, it shows how specific people and families could remain connected to local geography through the names recorded by others. Native Long Island history is not only about broad groups or territories, but also about named individuals, remembered places, and continuing community presence.

rows.title: Awixa Creek
rows.summary: Awixa is identified as a small stream in Islip near Bay Shore, between Penataquit Creek and Orawac Brook. The name also applied to the neck of land west of the creek, known in one early record as Aweeksa Neck.
rows.address_label: Awixa Creek, Bay Shore / Islip, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Awixa Creek preserves a Native name for a small Islip stream near Bay Shore, set among other named waterways such as Penataquit Creek and Orawac Brook. Interpretive context links Awixa to boundary or extent language, while the many related forms show how neighboring creek names could overlap in colonial records. South Shore streams marked movement, limits, agreements, and Native place memory.

rows.title: Ayeuonganit  Aunakésuck Muhhogkunk
rows.summary: Ayeuonganit Aunakésuck Muhhogkunk, also known as Burying Point, is a now desecrated 18th century Montaukett burying ground and arrowhead workshop. Both traditional stone grave markers and contemporary headstones were found and moved from the area for residential development.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Ayeuonganit Wampum Ayimꝏup
rows.summary: Ayeuonganit Wampum Ayimꝏup, also known through Parrish Pond, is remembered by Shinnecock people as a wampum-making place. Shinnecock activists defended the land from subdivision in February 2000, and Southampton Town preserved part of the cultural landscape in 2014.
rows.address_label: Parrish Pond / St. Andrews Circle area, Southampton (generalized)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Parrish Pond struggle shows how Shinnecock cultural knowledge and direct action protected land threatened by development. Its history centers living Shinnecock stewardship and the cultural work of wampum-making rather than treating wampum only as an object of the past.

rows.title: Bethel Christian ave., Laurel Hill Historic District
rows.summary: The Bethel-Christian Avenue-Laurel Hill Historic District (BCALH) was established and recognized by the Town of Brookhaven in 2005. It is a half-mile long stretch of Christian Avenue that includes the homes of several mixed heritage Native American and African American families as well as Bethel AME Church of Setauket, Laurel Hill Cemetery, and the Irving Hart Memorial Legion Hall. The BCALH was founded in response to the loss of the R.W. Hawkins house, a small 19th century cottage that was home to members of the.
rows.listing_image_alt: Bethel AME Historic District Setauket Christian Ave_5I5A0274 WEB
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Black Bank Hassock
rows.summary: Black Bank Hassock is the third of the grouped Hassock entries and is identified as another tract in the same East Rockaway Inlet locality as Great Bear Hassock.
rows.address_label: East Rockaway Inlet, Queens/Nassau County, New York
rows.why_this_matters: Black Bank Hassock preserves a meadow-name near East Rockaway Inlet, with the Hassock element connected to grass, sedge, or marsh land. That meaning points to the importance of South Shore wetlands as places of material knowledge, where grasses and sedges could support mats, coverings, and daily work. Marshes are culturally meaningful Native landscapes, not empty or marginal ground.

rows.title: Cachinncak / Orawac Brook
rows.summary: Orawac or Orowoc is a brook placename in Islip, connected with the modern Orowoc Creek and older Cachinncak boundary-marker name.
rows.address_label: Orowoc Creek / Orawac Brook, Bay Shore-East Islip, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Cachinncak / Orawac Brook preserves layered names for an Islip waterway now associated with Orowoc Creek, including language interpreted as a marked place or boundary. That meaning shows how brooks could serve as more than physical features: they could mark limits, guide movement, and organize land relationships. South Shore waterways remain part of Indigenous geography and memory, even when later English names such as Paper Mill Brook entered written sources.

rows.title: Canapaukah / Dutch Kills
rows.summary: Canapaukah is associated with Dutch Kills, the north branch of Newtown Creek in Long Island City. The early record identifies the waterway generally rather than a precise point.
rows.why_this_matters: Canapaukah preserves a Native name for the Dutch Kills branch of Newtown Creek, interpreted as a fenced or enclosed water-place. That meaning invites attention to water control, creek edges, and local observation in a landscape now heavily urbanized and industrial. Western Long Island and Queens remain part of Native geography, where older waterway names matter even when the shoreline has been dramatically changed.

rows.title: Canarsie
rows.summary: Canarsie is a western Long Island entry for the Native community and place name associated with Flatlands, Brooklyn, and nearby parts of Queens. The public marker remains approximate and educational, connecting early Dutch contact, place-name history, and later myths about Native disappearance without treating those myths as fact.
rows.address_label: Flatlands / Canarsie, Brooklyn, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Canarsie preserves a Native placename and community name in Brooklyn, reminding visitors that western Long Island is part of Indigenous Long Island history. The name is often connected with fenced or enclosed place meanings, while the exact original reference remains tied to careful reading of colonial records. Its survival in a modern urban neighborhood reveals Native geography beneath city maps and continued Indigenous presence rather than a distant or separate past.

rows.title: Canarsie Traditional Land
rows.summary: Canarsie homelands are remembered across present-day Brooklyn, Flatlands, Jamaica, the bay islands, and western Long Island. Early Dutch and English records place Canarsie people in relation to coastal villages, waterways, neighboring Native communities, land negotiations, and continued western Long Island Native presence.
rows.why_this_matters: Canarsie Traditional Land presents Brooklyn and western Long Island as Native homeland. The page connects place names, colonial records, Lenape-related language context, and public memory without reducing Canarsie history to a myth of disappearance.

rows.title: Canoe Place Chapel
rows.summary: Canoe Place Chapel, built around 1819-1820, is a surviving place connected with Shinnecock Christian worship and community life at Canoe Place. Its history belongs to a wider landscape shaped by Shinnecock land, Rev. Paul Cuffee's ministry, nineteenth-century religious change, and later preservation.
rows.address_label: 36 Canoe Place Rd, Hampton Bays, NY 11946
rows.listing_image_alt: Canoe Place Chapel and Graves_5I5A1199 WEB
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Canoe Place Chapel preserves a visible connection between Shinnecock community life and a place transformed by roads, rail, the canal, and land loss. The building also shows how Native Christian history can remain rooted in Indigenous kinship, land, and community authority.

rows.title: Cantasquntah
rows.summary: Cantasquntah is an Islip brook name associated with reeds and colonial boundary geography, with the exact modern creek course still treated cautiously.
rows.address_label: Islip village / Widow's Brook area, NY (general approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Cantasquntah preserves an Islip brook name interpreted as a great reed place or principal place of reeds. That meaning points to wetland plants as important materials for mats, coverings, and everyday work, not just background vegetation. Native placenames can record ecological knowledge, and South Shore brooks and marshes were part of lived Indigenous landscapes.

rows.title: Cantiague
rows.summary: Cantiague preserves Tooker's Cantiaque, Cantiagge, and Kiscasutta boundary-tree names for marked points of trees on the Hempstead and Oyster Bay plains. The modern marker is approximate, using the Cantiague Park area in Hicksville as a general location basis.
rows.address_label: Cantiague Park / Hicksville, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Cantiague preserves boundary-tree language from the Hempstead and Oyster Bay plains, with meanings tied to marked, chopped, or blazed trees. That detail matters because trees could function as public memory, navigation, and boundary markers in Native and colonial land records. Even suburban Nassau County landscapes carry older Indigenous systems of orientation and land relationship.

rows.title: Castateum
rows.summary: Castateum is an Indigenous placename recorded for salt meadows near Flatlands in Brooklyn. The marker represents the broader historic meadow landscape rather than a surveyed tract boundary.
rows.address_label: General Flatlands / Marine Park salt-meadow area, Brooklyn, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Castateum preserves a Native name for the Flatlands salt-meadow landscape and recalls the ecological and working importance of coastal grasslands before the modern Brooklyn shoreline took shape. The approximate marker keeps that history visible without pretending that the original meadow tract has been precisely surveyed.

rows.title: Cataconacke (Old Field)
rows.summary: Cataconacke, recorded by Tooker as Cataconnock, refers to Great Neck near Setauket, now known as Old Field. The existing map point marks the modern Old Field peninsula as a general location for the placename.
rows.address_label: 207 Old Field Rd, Setauket- East Setauket, NY 11733
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Cataconacke preserves a Setauket-area name for the Old Field peninsula, interpreted as a limited or enclosed place, land, or field. The meaning fits a neck of land bounded by water and shows how Native placenames could describe the shape and use of a landscape. North Shore peninsulas carry Native geographies and older names beneath later English estates and village landmarks.

rows.title: Caumsett
rows.summary: Caumsett names Lloyd Neck in Huntington and connects the peninsula with stone, shoreline, Native place knowledge, and seventeenth-century land records. Caumsett names Lloyd Neck in Huntington, a peninsula bounded by Oyster Bay, Cow Harbor, and Long Island Sound. The existing polygon is a modern outline for the neck, not a surveyed colonial boundary.
rows.address_label: Lloyd Neck / Caumsett State Historic Park Preserve, Lloyd Harbor, NY
rows.listing_image_alt: 1687 hand-drawn map of Lloyd Neck / Fort Neck meadows.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Caumsett preserves a Native name for Lloyd Neck, interpreted as a place near a sharp rock or whetstone-like stone. That meaning points to geology as part of Indigenous place knowledge: rocks were not just scenery, but useful materials connected to sharpening, work, and orientation. The North Shore appears here as a Native landscape where peninsulas, harbors, and stone resources were known and named with care.

rows.title: Caushawasha
rows.summary: A Southold swamp name on Hashamomuk Neck, likely preserving a Native personal name within wetland boundary records.
rows.address_label: Hashamomuk Neck, Southold, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Caushawasha appears to preserve a Native personal name connected with a swamp on Hashamomuk Neck, rather than a simple translated landform term. The general marker is intentionally approximate, but the name still points to wetlands with springs, brooks, shelter, and foodways that mattered in Native life. Southold's swamp and neck landscapes are places of community memory and continued Indigenous presence, not empty land between better-known landmarks.

rows.title: Chebiakinnausuk
rows.summary: A Montauk North Neck boundary-mark name from the 1670 Wuchebesuck purchase, shown only as a general approximation.
rows.address_label: North Neck, Montauk, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Chebiakinnausuk preserves boundary language from the 1670 Wuchebesuck purchase on Montauk's North Neck, with meanings such as marked separation or bound-mark. Its exact placement remains uncertain, but the name shows how boundaries could be named, marked, remembered, and later written into land agreements. Montaukett geography was a living framework of places and relationships, not simply lines imposed through colonial records.

rows.title: Checkachagin
rows.summary: An Oyster Bay waterway name preserved through place-name research, with an approximate Beaver Lake/Mill Neck marker rather than a traced brook line.
rows.address_label: Beaver Swamp Creek / Beaver Lake area, Mill Neck, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Checkachagin preserves a personal-name placename for an Oyster Bay brook flowing toward Beaver Swamp Creek, with records connecting it to Chechagon or Quaropin. The modern marker is approximate rather than a traced brook line, but the name still links a waterway to a remembered Native person and local community geography. Brook names can carry human history, not only descriptions of land and water.

rows.title: Chequit
rows.summary: Chequit is a Shelter Island placename for a point of land at Shelter Island Heights, later associated with Prospect, where the Shelter Island Heights Association developed a hotel and cottages.
rows.address_label: Chequit Point / Shelter Island Heights, Shelter Island, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Chequit preserves a Shelter Island point name whose translation remains uncertain and should not be forced into a weakfish explanation. That uncertainty matters because public history can respect Native language without pretending every surviving name has a simple English equivalent. The general Chequit Point location keeps Shelter Island's coastal geography connected to Indigenous Long Island memory while leaving room for what the records do not securely explain.

rows.title: Choppauhshapaugausuck
rows.summary: Choppauhshapaugausuck names the Montauk locality connected with the ditch or outlet of Great Pond on the south, the place from which Ditch Plain takes its English name.
rows.address_label: Ditch Plain / south outlet of Lake Montauk, Montauk, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Choppauhshapaugausuck preserves a Montauk placename tied to the outlet where water from Great Pond, now Lake Montauk, opened near Ditch Plain. Its interpretation connects hydrology, movement, and boundary-making. The exact historic outlet cannot be traced confidently across today's altered landscape.

rows.title: Circassian Shipwreck
rows.summary: On December 30th, 1876, freight ship Circassian wrecked off the coast of Mecox Bay in Bridgehampton. Ten members of the Shinnecock tribe were among those who drowned while attempting to rescue to ship's crew and cargo. Since the tragedy, the Shinnecock Nation has held remembrance gatherings that include drumming, dance, and feasting to remember ancestors who gave their lives to support their commu

rows.title: Columbus Day Monument Protest
rows.summary: A 1997 protest against the Christopher Columbus statue in Syracuse connected Chief Harry Wallace and Unkechaug activism to wider Indigenous challenges to public monuments that honor colonization.
rows.address_label: Columbus Circle, Syracuse, NY
rows.why_this_matters: This stop connects Long Island Native activism to broader struggles over public memory and monuments.

rows.title: Compowams
rows.summary: Compowams refers to a neck of land in Islip west of Bay Shore. Tooker also records the name for the brook along the neck, now known as Bay Shore Brook.
rows.address_label: Bay Shore Brook, Bay Shore, NY (approximate general location)
rows.why_this_matters: Compowams preserves a South Shore name applied to both a neck of land west of Bay Shore and the brook now known as Bay Shore Brook. The interpretation remains uncertain: the possessive form may point to a Native personal name, while other comparisons suggest meanings connected with closing or a doorway. One name can hold land, water, personhood, and unresolved language history together in a local place.

rows.title: Conegums
rows.summary: Conegums is a Mattituck creek name recorded by Tooker. He identifies the stream with Reeve's Creek, later known as James Creek, near the boundary between Southold and Riverhead.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Conegums preserves a Mattituck creek name interpreted as a boundary, identified with Reeve's Creek and later James Creek near the Southold-Riverhead line. As a named bound, the creek shows how waterways could organize land agreements, movement, and memory across the North Fork. Creeks were not minor features; they could mark limits, guide travel, and carry Native geography into later maps and town records.

rows.title: Connecticut (Carman's River)
rows.summary: Connecticut names a Brookhaven creek or river now known as Carman's River. The name appears in early Mastic-area boundary language and should not be confused with the New England river or the modern state.
rows.address_label: Carman's River, Brookhaven, NY (approximate general location)
rows.why_this_matters: Connecticut, as an early name for Carman's River, preserves a Native descriptor meaning at the long river or long tidal creek. The name shows that familiar Algonquian place-language could appear in multiple regions while still describing a specific Long Island waterway. Carman's River belongs to Indigenous geography as a named, remembered river, not only as a later colonial or modern landmark.

rows.title: Conscience Point
rows.summary: Conscience Point is remembered locally as the 1640 landing place of English settlers in Southampton, but the harbor and marsh landscape was already part of Shinnecock homeland. Its history should begin with Shinnecock presence, land use, diplomacy, and survival before turning to the English settlement story preserved by Southampton institutions.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Coopers Beach: Shinnecock Beach Access
rows.summary: Coopers Beach stands on the Atlantic shore of Shinnecock homeland. Shinnecock citizens have organized for free access after tribal members faced parking fees and tickets at a beach their families have used for generations. Their proposed solution is direct: recognize a Shinnecock tribal ID for free beach access and parking.
rows.address_label: Coopers Beach, 268 Meadow Lane, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.why_this_matters: Beach access is about more than parking. It concerns Shinnecock sovereignty, a continuing relationship with the Atlantic shore, and whether municipal rules recognize that Shinnecock people are not visitors to their own homeland. Accepting tribal ID would provide a clear, dignified way to restore access without forcing tribal citizens to buy permission to reach the coast.

rows.title: Copeces
rows.summary: Copeces is an Indigenous place name connected with a locality at the head of Three Mile Harbor in East Hampton. It is associated with Hand's Creek and the sheltered inner harbor area near Ashawagh.
rows.address_label: Hand's Creek / head of Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton, NY (approximate general location)

rows.title: Copiag
rows.summary: Copiag names a Babylon neck of land south of the old settlement of Breslau. The name survives in modern Copiague and Copiague Neck.
rows.address_label: Copiague Neck, Babylon, NY (approximate general location)

rows.title: Copwax
rows.summary: Copwax is a Rockaway Neck creek name recorded by Tooker. It appears in colonial land-paper context and is related to the earlier Coekwas spelling.
rows.address_label: Rockaway Neck, Queens, NY (approximate general location)

rows.title: Coram
rows.summary: Coram is a Brookhaven hamlet placename on the old country road, with related forms including Moncorum, Corum, Coraway, Puding, Wincoram, and Winecorum.
rows.address_label: Coram, Brookhaven, NY (approximate general location)

rows.title: Coram / Wincoram
rows.summary: Coram is represented here with the Wincoram and Winnecoram forms, tied to a Brookhaven place-name and a 1677 record of a pond in the woods.

rows.title: Corchaug Ancestral Land
rows.summary: The Corchaug name belongs to a North Fork homeland shaped by Peconic Bay, Long Island Sound, creeks, neck lands, and planting places. Colonial records connect Corchaug people with Southold/Yennecott, Orient Point, wampum, diplomacy, and growing land pressure after English settlement.
rows.why_this_matters: Corchaug Ancestral Land shows the North Fork as Native homeland, not only as a line of colonial towns. The name carries memory of Peconic waters, neck lands, wampum, diplomacy, land records, and community life across the eastern end of Long Island.

rows.title: Corchaug Tribe
rows.summary: Corchaug history belongs to the North Fork coastal world: Peconic estuaries, Long Island Sound, planting places, wampum, diplomacy, and pressure after English settlement. Corchaug people and places appear in records from the lands east of Setauket toward Orient Point, while sensitive locations remain protected.

rows.title: Council Rock
rows.summary: Council Rock is remembered in relation to Fort Hill Cemetery and a Montaukett meeting and burial landscape. Public mapping uses broad orientation only and does not identify graves, ceremony locations, the exact rock, or other sensitive details.
rows.address_label: Fort Hill Road area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Cove Realty Site
rows.summary: In 1952, The Great Cove Real Estate Company attempted to build houses on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation just south of Montauk Highway in an attempt to steal Shinnecock Land. The final court decision in 1961 resulted in success for the Shinnecock Tribe, preserving the land as part of the reservation. The foundations for the houses can still be seen today.
rows.address_label: Northern edge of the Shinnecock Reservation, south of Montauk Highway (generalized)

rows.title: Cumsewogue
rows.summary: Cumsewogue is a Brookhaven placename associated with the high plain south of Port Jefferson. It as a farming district and preserves it as a local name connected with movement across the land.
rows.address_label: Port Jefferson Station / Cumsewogue area, Town of Brookhaven, NY

rows.title: Cupsogue
rows.summary: Cupsogue is a coastal placename on Great South Beach opposite Eastport, with related recorded forms including Cupsage and Cupsawege.
rows.address_label: Cupsogue Beach / Great South Beach opposite Eastport, Town of Southampton, NY

rows.title: Cutchogue
rows.summary: Cutchogue is a Southold placename connected with the modern hamlet and an older Corchaug tract. It as a post-office and farming hamlet and notes that the name originally applied to land where a Corchaug village stood on Fort Neck. Quochague is a later record form treated as a Cutchogue cross-reference. The name is interpreted as the principal place.
rows.address_label: Cutchogue / Fort Neck, Town of Southold, NY

rows.title: Cutsgunsuck
rows.summary: Cutsgunsuck is Tooker's Indigenous placename for the brook or creek known in English as Stony Brook. The waterway marked part of the boundary between Brookhaven and Smithtown at the village of Stony Brook.
rows.address_label: Stony Brook waterway / Brookhaven-Smithtown boundary, NY

rows.title: December 1685 Deed
rows.summary: The December 1685 deed places John Mahue in direct negotiation with Governor Thomas Dongan over land between the Forge River and the Seatuck River. The deed belongs to a longer history of Unkechaug land pressure, colonial patents, and Native leaders navigating colonial legal systems.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Dickepechegans
rows.summary: Dickepechegans is Tooker's recorded Indigenous placename for the Huntington hills now known as Dix Hills. The modern name is explained through Dick Pechegan, whose home and planted fields were associated with the hills.
rows.address_label: Dix Hills, Town of Huntington, NY

rows.title: Duke Site
rows.summary: The Duke Site is associated with shell-midden archaeology near the Hands Creek and Ashawagh landscape. Public mapping gives only broad area context and does not identify shell midden locations, parcels, or routes.
rows.address_label: Hands Creek Road area

rows.title: Eastville
rows.summary: Eastville in Sag Harbor is a contemporary community shaped by free Black families, Native people, whalers, immigrants, and European settlers. In the nineteenth century, Sag Harbor offered work for Montaukett people and other Native maritime workers connected to the whaling economy.
rows.address_label: 139 Hampton St, Sag Harbor, NY 11963
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Elliott A. Brooks Carvings
rows.summary: Beginning in 1933, Elliott Alvah Brooks carved figures into shoreline boulders in Orient. The carvings, later called Bear Rock Studio, were cataloged as a memorial to Poquatuck people. Brooks was a non-Native artist and collector, so the place also raises questions about who interprets Indigenous history and how Native belongings were collected during the twentieth century.
rows.why_this_matters: The carvings preserve a local memory of Poquatuck people while showing the limits of memorials created through a non-Native collector's viewpoint. Their history invites a fuller account centered on Indigenous presence rather than disappearance.

rows.title: Equendito
rows.summary: Equendito is Tooker's recorded placename for Barren Island in Flatlands, Kings County. A 1664 deed identified the island by its Indigenous name and by the English name Broken Lands.
rows.address_label: Historic Barren Island / Floyd Bennett Field area, Flatlands, Brooklyn, NY

rows.title: Essachias / Wehahamis Creeks
rows.summary: Essachias is a small Islip creek name preserved by Tooker from a 1714 deed. The deed places it east of Great River and southeast of Brickkiln Point, paired with another small creek called Wehahamis.
rows.address_label: General Great River / East Islip waterfront area, Town of Islip, NY

rows.title: Fort Corchaug
rows.summary: Fort Corchaug is a seventeenth-century Indigenous fortified site on the North Fork connected with Corchaug community life, wampum production, diplomacy, trade, and the disruptions of Dutch and English colonial expansion. Archaeology suggests a double-palisade enclosure used during the contact period, but the fort also belongs to a longer Native landscape and community history.
rows.address_label: 23800 Main Rd, Cutchogue, NY 11935
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Fort Shinnecock
rows.summary: Fort Shinnecock marks a Shinnecock Hills landscape associated with a contact-period Shinnecock fort tradition and with June Meeting, a Native Christian gathering connected to Reverend John Cuffee and Eastern Long Island Native communities. Development has disrupted much of the historic landscape, so interpretation should remain careful, broad, and respectful.

rows.title: Fowler House
rows.summary: The Fowler House in Freetown belonged to Montaukett gardener George Lewis Fowler and Sarah Melissa Horton Fowler. Current architectural research indicates that the house was built in Freetown around 1885, after Montaukett families faced dispossession at Indian Field, rather than moved intact from Montauk.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Freetown
rows.summary: Freetown was a mixed-race community north of East Hampton, established before 1790. In the late nineteenth century, Arthur Benson offered Freetown plots to Montaukett people as part of the pressure to remove them from Montauk. The Fowler House remains in the area, while St. Matthew Chapel was moved.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Fresh Pond Fort
rows.summary: The Fresh Pond Fort is located on Montaukett territory on the east end of Long Island. The fort had already been in decay by the time of the English settlement in the area. No trace of this fort was found in a 1947 survey of the area by archaeologists Smith and Gaynell Stone. The setting of the locale is in a dense brush with scrub oaks, in a comparatively deserted section of Long Island near the Hither (Nominick) Hills.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Fresh Pond Site
rows.summary: Fresh Pond on Shelter Island is associated with archaeological evidence of shellfish processing, tools, pottery, fire-cracked rock, and repeated seasonal or year-round occupation. Its specific archaeological deposits are not publicly identified.
rows.address_label: Fresh Pond, Shelter Island, New York (approximate public area)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Garvie's Point Site
rows.summary: The Garvies Point Site featured a once exposed archaic shell midden found on an eroding bluff. During 20th century excavations, among the objects found in the shell deposit were a semi-lunar knife or ulu of ground blue slate, a large slate projectile point, a broken chisel, and a bannerstone or atlatl weight, each from the archaic period. The site appeared to be pre-pottery characteristic of the archaic period.
rows.address_label: Garvies Point Museum and Preserve, Glen Cove, New York (public museum area)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Shell middens and Archaic-period tools at Garvie's Point place Native Long Island in deep time, through generations of Indigenous knowledge, coastal foodways, and careful use of local stone, shellfish, and shoreline environments. The lesson is also about protection: erosion, development, and collecting have damaged many coastal archaeological places. Learning from the public museum and preserve should build respect for Native continuity and for the responsibility to preserve what remains.

rows.title: Georgica
rows.summary: Georgica is an East Hampton placename associated with the farming district between East Hampton village and Wainscott and with Georgica Pond. Tooker traces the name through seventeenth-century records and local tradition.
rows.address_label: Georgica Pond area, East Hampton, NY

rows.title: Gid's Island Fort
rows.summary: Gid's Island Fort is remembered through nineteenth-century local history rather than through a clearly preserved archaeological site. Benjamin F. Thompson mentioned the North Fork fort in his 1843 History of Long Island, making Thompson's account important but limited by the perspective of later writers.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Gilgo
rows.summary: Gilgo is a Babylon barrier-beach placename for an inlet from the ocean to Great South Bay, placed between Oak Island and Jones Beach in the source record.
rows.address_label: Gilgo Beach / Gilgo Inlet area, Town of Babylon, NY

rows.title: Gonux
rows.summary: Gonux is a Southold placename for a point on Great Hog Neck, also called Peconic Park. the point was named for Moses Gonack, who drowned nearby and was buried there.
rows.address_label: Great Hog Neck / Peconic Park, Town of Southold, NY

rows.title: Gowanus
rows.summary: Gowanus is a Brooklyn placename for the historic creek, bay, and locality recorded in early Dutch colonial records as Gowanus, Gowanes, and Gouwanes.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Gravesend Road Burial Protection Protest
rows.summary: The Gravesend Road protest connected Shinnecock and Montaukett community action with the protection of Native burial places in Brooklyn.
rows.address_label: Montauk, East Hampton (generalized)
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock and Montaukett community action at Gravesend Road demonstrates that protecting burial places is an ongoing form of Indigenous activism. The location remains intentionally broad to protect burials, sacred places, and private land.

rows.title: Great Bear Hassock
rows.summary: Great Bear Hassock is one of three Hassock entries grouped around Rockaway and East Rockaway Inlet. It is identified as a tract of meadow near East Rockaway Inlet.
rows.address_label: East Rockaway Inlet, Queens/Nassau County, New York

rows.title: Gueguis
rows.summary: A Babylon placename for Little Neck, recorded in an August 1696 deed and generally associated with the necks south of Lindenhurst/Breslau.
rows.address_label: General Little Neck area south of Lindenhurst, Town of Babylon, NY

rows.title: Gunnunks
rows.summary: Gunnunks is a Montauk North Neck placename for a swamp and nearby tract called Gunnunk's Garden, placed midway between Fort Pond and Culloden Point, at the foot of Rocky Ridge.
rows.address_label: General North Neck / Rocky Ridge area, Montauk, NY

rows.title: Guscomquorom
rows.summary: A Babylon neck name interpreted as a crossing place, linking Great East Neck with trail or wading-place memory toward Santapaug.
rows.address_label: General Great East Neck area, West Babylon, NY

rows.title: Hallock Site
rows.summary: The Hallock Site is associated with a seventeenth-century stone-working and village landscape. Its precise archaeological deposits are not publicly identified.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Halsey Homestead
rows.summary: A Southampton homesite tied to difficult colonial records about land pressure, Native diplomacy, and later interpretations of Shinnecock and Montaukett authority.
rows.address_label: 249 S Main St #4826, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Halsey Homestead story is often repeated through colonial language that can make Native people appear violent and faceless. A fuller reading shows a crisis shaped by settlement expansion, colonial punishment, uncertain records, Shinnecock leadership, Montaukett diplomacy, and Native people making difficult decisions under pressure.

rows.title: Hashamomuk
rows.summary: Hashamomuk is William Wallace Tooker's name for a neck of land west of Greenport in Southold. Later entries connect the place with Nashayonsuck, a brook-boundary name, and with neighboring Southold forms such as Monnepaught and Caushawasha.
rows.address_label: Hashamomuk / Arshamomaque area west of Greenport, Southold, NY

rows.title: Hassock (Rockaway Beach)
rows.summary: Hassock is recorded by Tooker as a creek in the meadow near Rockaway Beach. The exact creek has not been identified, but the name is associated broadly with the Rockaway Beach marsh landscape.
rows.address_label: Rockaway Beach, Queens County, New York

rows.title: Hassockey / Jamaica Meadows
rows.summary: Hassockey is a name preserved in early Jamaica records for marshy meadow localities. Because the records describe more than one tract, the marker is intentionally approximate.
rows.address_label: General Jamaica / South Jamaica marsh landscape, Queens, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: Hassockey keeps early Jamaica wetland geography visible in a landscape heavily altered by drainage and development. Its plural documentary use also shows why a historical place name may need a broad marker rather than a false single-site precision.

rows.title: Hauppauge
rows.summary: Hauppauge is identified as a hamlet on the southern border of Smithtown. The name is connected to the swampy headwaters that feed Winganhauppauge Brook rather than to the popular explanation of sweet water.
rows.address_label: Hauppauge, Suffolk County, New York

rows.title: Hawthorne Site
rows.summary: In August 2018, human remains were uncovered during residential development on Hawthorne Road in Shinnecock Hills. Shinnecock leaders objected to further disturbance and called for proper treatment of a possible ancestral burial place while review was pending.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Hempstead Plains Deed Landscape, 1643
rows.summary: Merrick, Merriack, and Meroke records are connected to the 1643 Hempstead purchase, described as part of the great plain toward the south side. The transaction involved English purchasers Robert Fordham and John Carman and Native leaders associated with Massapequa, Merrick, and Rockaway communities. This deed landscape points to different understandings of land, use, authority, and ownership that shaped later dispossession.
rows.address_label: Hempstead Plains / south side landscape, Town of Hempstead
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as one of the communities named in the Hempstead deed tradition.
rows.why_this_matters: The 1643 Hempstead Plains record is a key entry point into Merrick land loss. It presents dispossession as a legal, ecological, and community transformation across Native homelands.

rows.title: Hocum
rows.summary: Hocum is a corrected placename for a location on or near Secatogue Neck in West Islip, possibly a chief's name or a hook-shaped feature rather than the name of the whole neck.
rows.address_label: Secatogue Neck / West Islip, Suffolk County, New York

rows.title: Hoggenoch
rows.summary: Hoggenoch is a correction, not a traditional Indigenous placename. The form was applied to Little Hog Neck near Sag Harbor and came from a mistaken spelling of Hog Neck in the 1686 Dongan Patent for Southampton.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Hoggenoch - Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Hoggenoch - Manhansett Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Hoggenoch should not be presented as a traditional Indigenous placename. The form is identified as a mistaken spelling of Hog Neck in the 1686 Dongan Patent for Southampton, applied to Little Hog Neck near Sag Harbor.

rows.title: Homes Hill
rows.summary: Homes Hill is recorded as a hill at North Sea in Southampton.
rows.address_label: Homes Hill / North Sea Harbor, Southampton, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Hoopaninak
rows.summary: Hoopaninak is recorded by William Wallace Tooker as an island at Flatlands in Kings County. The name appears in a 1664 deed for upland, marshes, beaches, and an adjoining island described as enclosed by the ocean sea.
rows.address_label: Flatlands / Jamaica Bay, Brooklyn, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Horse Barn Burial Site
rows.summary: In 2003, a group burial was discovered during residential development and barn construction on Shelter Island, dating between about 1400 and 1640. Shinnecock tribal members argued against further disturbance and treated the area as a cemetery. Despite their resistance, development continued, and the remains were reburied in an undisclosed location on Shelter Island.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Howell Homestead
rows.summary: In 1657, houses were burned in Southampton village by two Shinnecock men and a black woman who served in one of the houses belonging to Eleanor Howell, widow of Edward Howell a founder of the town. The motive may have been in retaliation for the mistreatment of servants in the Howell home, or in response to roaming horses from Southampton destroying Shinnecock corn fields Colonial authorities in Hartford sent a troop of nineteen men under the command of John Mason, who commanded the massacre of the Pequot at.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Ihpetonga
rows.summary: Ihpetonga is recorded by William Wallace Tooker as a name bestowed on Brooklyn Heights by Henry R. Schoolcraft. It is presented here as a descriptive name for the heights or high sandy banks of the Brooklyn bluff.
rows.address_label: Brooklyn Heights, Brooklyn, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Indian Field Cemetery
rows.summary: Indian Field Cemetery is a traditional Montaukett burial ground in East Hampton. Public mapping gives broad cemetery orientation only and does not identify unmarked graves or sensitive details.
rows.address_label: East Lake Drive area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Indian Fields
rows.summary: Indian Fields is a Montaukett homeland at Montauk with evidence of long Native occupation, homesteads, ponds, bluffs, and coastal lifeways. The place is central to Montaukett history before and after the Benson-era dispossession that pushed many Montaukett families west while community identity and memory continued.
rows.address_label: Montauk, East Hampton
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Indian Island Site
rows.summary: In 2005, storm erosion at Indian Island County Park exposed ancestral burial material and artifacts. Shinnecock and Unkechaug people worked with public officials around repatriation and protection. Precise exposure locations remain withheld to protect ancestral burials.

rows.title: Jabash
rows.summary: Jabash is a Shinnecock Neck placename recorded by William Wallace Tooker for a cove on the east side of the neck. one Native resident on the neck called it Irabash cove.
rows.address_label: East side of Shinnecock Neck, Southampton, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Jamaica
rows.summary: Jamaica is a Queens placename preserved through early town and purchase records.
rows.address_label: Jamaica / Beaver Pond vicinity, Queens, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Jamesport Site
rows.summary: The Jamesport Site is an Orient Period (1,000-1,300 BC) ceremonial burial ground. Archaeological work documented red ochre, burial offerings, and deliberately broken stone vessels associated with ceremonial practice. Riverhead Town purchased the land in 2017 because of its cultural significance and the need for protection.

rows.title: Jason's Rock
rows.summary: Jason's Rock is a large glacial boulder in Northwest Woods remembered through stories of a Montaukett traveler named Jason who paused there on journeys between East Hampton and Sag Harbor. The place connects Native movement, rest, water, and memory in the local landscape.

rows.title: Jones Beach Drift Whale Rights
rows.summary: Records connect Tackapousha and Native communities with asserted rights to valuable marine resources, including drift whales along the south shore barrier beaches. The modern Jones Beach landscape is therefore also a place to discuss Native jurisdiction, marine economies, and colonial legal change.
rows.address_label: Jones Beach barrier beach landscape, Jones Inlet vicinity
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of the south shore/barrier beach history; also connected with Massapequa leadership and overlapping regional authority.
rows.why_this_matters: Jones Beach is usually remembered as a modern public beach, but older records connect the barrier island to Native marine rights and coastal economies. The site carries histories of Indigenous jurisdiction and resource knowledge within a familiar public landscape.

rows.title: Kantuck
rows.summary: Kantuck is recorded as a locality in Oyster Bay, historically in Queens County and now in Nassau County. The place is described as wild, hilly, and swampy land at the head of a broad salt meadow.
rows.address_label: Beaver Swamp Creek / Mill Neck, Oyster Bay, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Kanungum / Conungum
rows.summary: Kanungum is a Calverton-area placename in Riverhead, also recorded as Conungum or Conungam and interpreted as a boundary enclosed place or boundary village.
rows.address_label: Calverton, Riverhead, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Keemiscomock
rows.summary: Keemiscomock is recorded by William Wallace Tooker as a small brook dividing the shores of Saghtekoos, also known as Apple Tree Neck, in Islip. The same brook was also called Weepoose.
rows.address_label: Sagtikos / Apple Tree Neck, Islip, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Keskaechqueren
rows.summary: Keskaechqueren, also recorded as Keskaechquerem, was a Canarsie village near Flatlands in Brooklyn and is interpreted through language for a gathering place.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Ketanomocke
rows.summary: Ketanomocke, also written Ketewamoke and Ketan-om-muck, is associated with Huntington and interpreted as a shoreline or beach placename.
rows.address_label: General Huntington / East Northport area, Suffolk County, New York

rows.title: Ketchaponack
rows.summary: Ketchaponack is a Southampton placename for a neck of land in the Westhampton Beach area, in the western part of Southampton town on Quantuck Creek near the historic West Hampton post office area.
rows.address_label: General Ketchaponack / Quantuck Creek area, Westhampton Beach, New York

rows.title: Ketumpscut / Catumb Reef
rows.summary: Ketumpscut is a Fishers Island-area placename connected with Catumb Reef, now identified as Catumb Rocks in the reef complex east of Fishers Island. Catumb and Ketumpscut are cross-referenced names for the same rocky offshore place.
rows.address_label: Catumb Rocks / Catumb Reef, reef complex east of Fishers Island between Sugar Reef and Lords Passage

rows.title: Killis
rows.summary: Killis is a Bridgehampton pond placename that survives in the modern Kellis Pond name. The pond is recorded, and its name is connected with a Native person who lived near the water, while also noting later spellings and family-name forms.
rows.address_label: Kellis Pond, Bridgehampton, New York

rows.title: Kioshk / Ellis Island
rows.summary: Kioshk is the recorded name for Ellis Island in New York Harbor. The source record is careful that this was not presented as an older local deed name; Henry R. Schoolcraft applied the Chippewa-derived name to the island in 1845.
rows.address_label: Ellis Island, New York Harbor

rows.title: Kissena Pond
rows.summary: Kissena is the recorded name for a pond at Flushing in Queens. The source immediately cautions that it is not an original Long Island name, but a later name applied to a body of water now associated with Kissena Park.
rows.address_label: Kissena Lake / Kissena Park, Flushing, Queens, New York

rows.title: Kitchaminchok
rows.summary: A Moriches Island boundary placename appearing in seventeenth-century whaling and estate records, with related forms including Ketchininchoge and Cochiminchoake.
rows.address_label: Moriches Island, Moriches Bay, East Moriches, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Konkhunganik
rows.summary: Konkhunganik is the recorded name for the southern part of Fort Pond at Montauk. In the deed language he cites, Fort Pond is described with Quanuntowunk on the north and Konkhunganik on the south.
rows.address_label: Southern Fort Pond, Montauk, New York

rows.title: Lake Agawam
rows.summary: Lake Agawam is the modern Southampton pond connected with the Agawom or Agawam entry. The broader application of Agawam to Southampton is presented as a historical error rather than a secure local Indigenous placename. The more specific place is the town pond in Southampton Village, while earlier writers mistakenly applied Agawam to the whole town.
rows.address_label: Lake Agawam, Southampton Village, NY

rows.title: Little Church
rows.summary: Around 1844, the “ Little Church ” is built on the reservation. It was a Millerite Church, a branch of the 7th day Adventist Congregationalist church. The Millerites were part of the great revival from upstate NY. Today, there is little evidence of the church beyond photographs.

rows.title: Ma's House
rows.summary: Ma's House & BIPOC Art Studio is a Native-led arts organization and community space on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation. Founded by Shinnecock artist and photographer Jeremy Dennis, the project began in June 2020 and became a New York nonprofit in 2021. The family house supports artist residencies, exhibitions, a shared studio and library, and art and history programs for the Shinnecock community and visiting artists.
rows.address_label: 159 Old Point Road, Southampton, NY 11969
rows.activity_update_summary: Added the 2022 John Jermain Memorial Library donation of more than 400 Native American books, including a link to Ma's House's searchable online catalog.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: On Shinnecock ancestral land / Shinnecock Indian Reservation.

rows.title: Macutteris
rows.summary: Macutteris is a Flatlands placename identified from a May 13, 1664 deed for upland and marshes in what is now Brooklyn. It appears in the same deed context as Hoopaninak and Shanscomacocke.
rows.address_label: General Flatlands / Jamaica Bay marsh area, Brooklyn, New York

rows.title: Madnans / Madnank
rows.summary: Madnans or Madnank carries an uncertain Great Neck place-name history, with a possible hilly-place interpretation in older records.
rows.address_label: General Great Neck peninsula, North Hempstead, New York

rows.title: Mahchongitchuge
rows.summary: Mahchongitchuge is a Montauk North Neck swamp name recorded from the 1670 deed for the land between the ponds. The deed places it in a boundary sequence running through the swamp toward Great Pond.
rows.address_label: General North Neck swamp area between Fort Pond and Great Pond / Lake Montauk

rows.title: Makeopaca
rows.summary: Makeopaca is a Gravesend placename from a July 1684 land transfer, with Moeung marking the eastward end of the beach in the boundary description.
rows.address_label: General Gravesend / Strome Kill area, Brooklyn, New York

rows.title: Mamanock Neck
rows.summary: Mamanock names a neck of land at East Moriches in Brookhaven. The cited records place Mamanock with Meritces, or Moriches Neck, suggesting a connected pair of necks along the south shore.
rows.address_label: General Mamanock Neck / East Moriches shoreline, New York

rows.title: Manantic / Menantic Creek
rows.summary: Manantic names a neck and creek in the western part of Shelter Island. The same source notes that Shelter Island people pronounced and spelled the name locally as Menantic.
rows.address_label: General Menantic Creek / Menantic Neck area, Shelter Island, New York

rows.title: Manchonack / Gardiners Island
rows.summary: Manchonack is Tooker's placename for Gardiners Island in East Hampton. The name appears in the 1639 deed by Yovawan, sachem of Pommanocc, and Aswaw to Lion Gardiner. The name is interpreted as a land of the departed.
rows.address_label: Gardiners Island, East Hampton, New York

rows.title: Manetuck
rows.summary: An Islip neck name connected with the 1701 Watchogue sale and an interpretation as a pine or cedar swamp.
rows.address_label: General West Bay Shore / Islip neck area, New York

rows.title: Manhansack-aqua-quash-awamock
rows.summary: Manhansack-aqua-quash-awamock is a Shelter Island placename associated with Manhanset history and seventeenth-century records. The existing polygon represents Shelter Island as a broad place association rather than an exact historic boundary.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Manhansett Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Manhansett records and community memory tie Shelter Island to Peconic water routes, island homelands, and sensitive descendant histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Manhansett Ancestral Land presents Shelter Island as Native homeland with its own language, records, and community memory. Broad territory pages need care when related places include sensitive burial and descendant histories.

rows.title: Manhansuck (Pipe's Neck Creek)
rows.summary: Manhansuck is a Southold placename for Pipe's Neck Creek, just west of Greenport. The name belongs to a creek and outlet setting near Pipe's Cove.
rows.address_label: Pipe's Cove / Pipe's Neck Creek, west of Greenport

rows.title: Manhasset
rows.summary: Manhasset names the village and neck formerly called Cow Neck in present-day Nassau County.
rows.address_label: Manhasset, Nassau County

rows.title: Manhattan
rows.summary: Manhattan is included among Long Island and adjacent island Native place names. Because Manhattan sits in Lenape/Munsee language territory, the name should not be flattened into a generic Algonquian label. The blue marker orients readers to the modern island, not an exact historic site.
rows.address_label: Manhattan Island, New York City
rows.why_this_matters: Manhattan preserves an Indigenous name at the center of one of the world's most familiar cityscapes. Later printed spellings and translations are partial evidence rather than final meanings. The name continues to point toward Lenape presence, language, and relationships with this island.

rows.title: Manitou Hill
rows.summary: Manitou Hill, also recorded as Mannatto, is the Manetto Hill ridge area in Plainview/Oyster Bay. The placename is connected with a 1695 deed and interpreted through the Manitto, or Great Spirit, tradition.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Manittuwond / Plum Island
rows.summary: An eastern island place name connected with older Indigenous fishing and planting memory around the Long Island Sound and Pequot region.
rows.address_label: Plum Island, Town of Southold

rows.title: Mannahanning / Coney Island
rows.summary: A Coney Island name from Kings County, shown as a modern orientation point rather than an exact 1654 deed boundary.
rows.address_label: Coney Island, Brooklyn

rows.title: Manor of St. George
rows.summary: Established in 1696 by Colonel William Tangier Smith, the Manor of St. George sits on Unkechaug homelands and is deeply tied to the early colonial economy of Long Island. Smith documented labor transactions with Unkechaug Native whalers and workers in The Pigskin Book (1696–1721), a record that reveals how Indigenous labor and maritime knowledge sustained coastal industries during a period of near-shore whaling carried out in small cedar boats. After Smith’s death, the ledger continued with indenture agreements.

rows.title: Manowtassquot / Namkee Creek
rows.summary: Manowtassquot and Namkee name creek-boundary geography west of Blue Point. The Namkee entry connects the creek mouth with fishing-place language and a remembered fishing-weir setting.
rows.address_label: General Corey Creek / Namkee Creek boundary area west of Blue Point

rows.title: Mantoobaugs
rows.summary: Mantoobaugs is Tooker's name for a reserved parcel on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold, associated with swamps, corn fields, and the Five Wigwams area. The blue marker is approximate.
rows.address_label: General Hashamomuk Neck / Arshamomaque area near Greenport

rows.title: Manunkquiaug
rows.summary: Manunkquiaug is a Montauk placename in the North Neck area, near Great Pond, now Lake Montauk. It appears as a boundary point in a 1670 Montauk deed.
rows.address_label: General eastern/southern Great Pond (Lake Montauk) boundary area

rows.title: Marechkawick
rows.summary: Marechkawick names a Native village associated with the site of Brooklyn in early Dutch colonial records. Recorded spellings include Marychkenwikingh, Merechkawick, Merchkawikingh, and Rechkewick. Reckkewick is a cross-reference form associated with the same Brooklyn landscape.

rows.title: Marratooka
rows.summary: Marratooka is a Mattituck placename for a pond and the farm bordering it in Southold town. The history gives Marritook as a related form and treats Marratooka as a later form connected with Mattituck.

rows.title: Mashashimuet
rows.summary: Mashashimuet names the springs on the south side of Otter Pond in Sag Harbor. The place is associated with today's Mashashimuet Park and Otter Pond landscape, and the name was remembered through Montaukett and local Native knowledge shared with William Wallace Tooker.

rows.title: Mashmanock
rows.summary: Mashmanock is a Southampton placename connected with Canoe Place Creek near the Canoe Place isthmus and Shinnecock Canal. The name is also cross-referenced to Mashomuck, and a later Toyonge entry creates a location question by associating the 1648 deed reference with Red Creek.

rows.title: Mashomuck
rows.summary: Mashomuck is a Shelter Island placename for the southern neck and point opposite Sag Harbor, now associated with Mashomack Preserve. Recorded forms include Meshomac, Marshammock, Mashomuk, Mashomuck, and the local pronunciation Mashom-uk.

rows.title: Maskachoung / Maskutchoung
rows.summary: Maskachoung, also written Maskutchoung, is recorded as a Native placename associated with a neck of land on the southern part of the Hempstead Plains. Strong discusses George Weeks's listing of Maskutchoung as a Native community near Hempstead. The name is interpreted as a grassland or prairie place.
rows.address_label: Southern Hempstead Plains / East Meadow area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as an interior Hempstead Plains placename and Native community reference near the south shore homeland.
rows.why_this_matters: Maskachoung shows that Merrick ancestral land was not only shoreline and bay. The Hempstead Plains were also Native geography, remembered through names for grassland, prairie, community, and movement between the interior and the south shore.

rows.title: Maspeth / Mespaetches
rows.summary: Maspeth, recorded in older forms such as Mespaetches, is a Queens placename tied to Newtown Creek and its former swamp landscape.

rows.title: Massabarkem (Gravesend Neck)
rows.summary: Massabarkem is a Gravesend Neck placename in Kings County, connected with a 1650 confirmatory deed and related forms later discussed as Maseebackhun or Massebackhun.

rows.title: Massakack (Half Hollow Hills)
rows.summary: A Huntington hills placename, also written Massaback, translated as great hill land.

rows.title: Massapeoque Meadows / South Oyster Bay
rows.summary: Massapeoque and Massapequa records preserve references to meadow landscapes and south shore salt meadows. These records point to wetlands as named, used, and negotiated places, not marginal land. The South Oyster Bay meadow landscape was part of hunting, fishing, shellfishing, travel, and later colonial claims over land and resources.
rows.address_label: South Oyster Bay marsh and meadow landscape, Massapequa-Seaford area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land with note that Massapequa and Merrick histories overlap across the south shore.
rows.why_this_matters: Massapeoque Meadows presents wetlands as Indigenous homelands and working landscapes. Salt meadows supported hunting, fishing, shellfishing, travel, and later colonial claims over land and resources.

rows.title: Massapequa Ancestral Lands
rows.summary: Massapequa and Massapeague histories connect South Oyster Bay, Fort Neck, diplomacy, defense, waterways, and land struggle across neighboring south shore communities.
rows.why_this_matters: Massapequa Ancestral Lands centers South Oyster Bay and Fort Neck as Native homeland and a place of diplomacy, defense, waterways, and land struggle. Massapequa, Merrick, Secatogue, Rockaway, and neighboring histories are often connected through these waters, records, and relationships.

rows.title: Massapequas
rows.summary: Massapequas connects Massapequa territory with south shore shell-heap and homeland context. The map placement is approximate and avoids archaeological, burial, residential, or looting-risk locations.
rows.address_label: Massapequa south shore territory, Nassau County, New York (approximate public area)

rows.title: Massapootupaug
rows.summary: Massapootupaug is a western Southampton placename connected with a 1662 Shinnecock conveyance boundary near Niamack, Canoe Place, and the old gutt.

rows.title: Massepe (Thurston's Creek)
rows.summary: Massepe is a Jamaica, Queens placename for a river or creek, probably the waterway later known as Thurston's Creek or Thurston Basin.

rows.title: Mastic
rows.summary: Mastic is a Brookhaven placename associated with the Mastic Peninsula and especially the Forge River, interpreted as a great river or great tidal river.
rows.address_label: General Forge River / Mastic Peninsula area, Brookhaven, NY

rows.title: Matanucke (Staten Island)
rows.summary: This Staten Island entry gathers related names discussed in Tooker, including Matanucke, Monocknong, and Aquehonga Manacknong. Monocknong is treated here as a cross-reference variant, not as a separate mapped site.

rows.title: Matinecock Town Hall Confrontation
rows.summary: In 1969, Princess Sun Tama (Ann Harding Murdock), Lee Canevari, Janet Hannani, and the Matinecock Indian Council confronted Huntington officials over Matinecock land claims and recognition. They challenged the town's reliance on colonial deeds and insisted that Matinecock title, memory, and political identity did not depend on whether officials acknowledged it.
rows.address_label: Huntington Town Hall, Huntington
