rows.why_this_matters: This stop shows municipal confrontation as a form of Native political action and land-claim advocacy.

rows.title: Matinecock Traditional Land
rows.summary: Matinecock homelands are remembered along the North Shore through harbors, necks, islands, village places, and land records. The name also carries living community identity, so this territory is best understood as both historical geography and continuing Native presence rather than only a colonial-map label.
rows.why_this_matters: Matinecock Traditional Land presents the North Shore as Native geography shaped by hills, harbors, observation places, travel, diplomacy, and continuing community memory.

rows.title: Matinecock Tribal Nation
rows.summary: The Matinecock Nation, an Algonquian people, has been the steward of northwestern Long Island since time immemorial. Their name, meaning “at the hilly land,” reflects an ancestral relationship with a territory extending along the North Shore from Flushing Bay to the Nissequogue River in present-day Smithtown. Long before European contact, Matinecock ancestors lived in extensive villages at Flushing, Port Washington, Glen Cove, Oyster Bay, Cold Spring Harbor, Huntington, and Northport, where numerous village sites.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Matinecock Way
rows.summary: Matinecock Way is the co-name adopted in 2015 for the intersection of Northern Boulevard and Marathon Parkway in Little Neck. The name honors continuing Matinecock presence and the Native history of northeastern Queens without treating that history as belonging only to the past.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Matinecock Way places a Native community name in the everyday geography of Little Neck. Matinecock people were present at the 2015 unveiling, and the co-name recognizes that their relationship to Queens and Long Island continues.

rows.title: Matowcas (Brooklyn)
rows.summary: Matowcas is a Brooklyn-area placename and broader territory name connected with the Native sachemdom associated with what became Brooklyn.

rows.title: Mattawommax (Probable Fireplace Meadow)
rows.summary: Mattawommax named a meadow locality in Brookhaven. Brookhaven's early town records place John Thompson's numbered meadow share in the 1664 Old Purchase at South, the landscape now associated with Brookhaven Hamlet, Bellport, and Fireplace Neck; the marker is a broad probable placement rather than an identified lot boundary.
rows.address_label: Fireplace Neck, Brookhaven, NY (probable broad landscape)
rows.why_this_matters: Mattawommax preserves a Native name within the salt-meadow geography that drew Setauket proprietors to Brookhaven's south shore. Linking the deed to the Old Purchase at South makes the record visible while the probable label keeps a numbered colonial share from being mistaken for an exact recovered Native boundary.

rows.title: Mattemoy (Mastic Neck)
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker links Mattemoy with one of the smaller necks of Mastic in Brookhaven. The name also appears as Mottemog in Long Island historical writing.

rows.title: Matthabanks (Great South Beach)
rows.summary: Matthabanks is a placename for the Great South Beach opposite Brookhaven, on the barrier island now generally known as Fire Island.

rows.title: Mattituck
rows.summary: Mattituck is the name of a village, bay, and creek in Southold. The placename remains attached to a living North Fork hamlet and its surrounding waterways.

rows.title: Mattock (North Sea Swamp)
rows.summary: Mattock is connected with a swamp near North Sea in Southampton. The name appears in eighteenth-century local records and may preserve either a description of swampy land or a personal name.

rows.title: Mattuck Brook (East Moriches)
rows.summary: Mattuck is a small brook at East Moriches in Brookhaven. The brook is tied to Watchogue, a neck of land forming the eastern section of East Moriches.

rows.title: Mechawanienck (New Utrecht)
rows.summary: Mechawanienck is a locality in Kings County. The name appears in a New Utrecht deed describing land running from Gouwanis across the hills toward the southeast side of Amersfoort, or Flatlands.

rows.title: Mechowodt Treaty and Reserved Rights Landscape, 1639
rows.summary: A 1639 Dutch agreement associated with Mechowodt of the Massapequa/Marossepinck world describes Native people reserving rights to remain on the land, plant corn, fish, hunt, and make a living there.
rows.address_label: South shore landscape, Rockaway-to-Suffolk treaty context
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of a broader south shore diplomatic and land-rights context involving overlapping Native polities.
rows.why_this_matters: The Mechowodt agreement complicates simple stories of land "sale." It shows Native leaders negotiating continued use and presence, and it helps explain how colonial legal records could both preserve Native claims and become instruments of dispossession.

rows.title: Mecox (Bridgehampton)
rows.summary: Meacox is connected with a farming district and inland bay at Bridgehampton. The modern spelling Mecox remains attached to Mecox Bay and the surrounding Bridgehampton landscape.

rows.title: Meitowax (Long Island)
rows.summary: Meitowax is a Long Island-wide name connected with map, patent, and historical variants including Matouwac, Metoac, Matowcas, Mattanwake, and Matowa.

rows.title: Memanusack (Stony Brook)
rows.summary: Memanusack, also recorded as Memanusuck, is connected with the stream from which Stony Brook takes its name. The waterway is described as an outlet from a pond into the harbor.

rows.title: Merikoke and Massapequa Shared Lands
rows.summary: The Merikoke/Merrick and Massapequa histories overlap across the south shore corridor, where source research describes kinship, refuge, shared territory, and alliance under colonial pressure.
rows.address_label: Merrick-Bellmore-Freeport south shore corridor
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land with recognition of overlapping Merikoke/Merrick and Massapequa histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Merikoke and Massapequa shared-land history challenges simple map boundaries. It shows Native communities responding to displacement through kinship, alliance, refuge, and shared use of south shore homelands.

rows.title: Merrick (Hempstead Plains)
rows.summary: Merrick is a Hempstead-area placename connected with the great plain south of Hempstead and later Merrick community names.

rows.title: Merrick Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Merrick and Merikoke homelands are remembered around the Hempstead plains, south shore bays, creeks, meadows, shellfish waters, planting grounds, and travel routes. The name appears in colonial and later sources in several spellings, including Merrick, Meroke, Merikoke, Mericoke, Merriack, Merricock, and Mercock.
rows.address_label: Broad Merrick / Freeport / Bellmore / Hempstead Plains and south shore wetland landscape, Nassau County, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Primary Merrick ancestral land record for related south shore and Hempstead Plains related south shore and Hempstead Plains entries.
rows.why_this_matters: Merrick Ancestral Land presents Nassau County's south shore as Native homeland: a place of language, plains, creeks, shellfish waters, travel routes, diplomacy, and continuing memory. The Merrick/Meroke references also shows that colonial land loss was contested. Native leaders and communities remained active in negotiations, legal challenges, kinship networks, and public memory long after early deeds were written.

rows.title: Merrick Neck Lands and Bay Villages
rows.summary: Merrick histories describe villages on south shore necks of land along the Great South Bay, tying Merrick and nearby Freeport-area community life to bays, meadows, creeks, fishing, shellfishing, travel, and archaeological memory.
rows.address_label: South shore neck lands, Merrick-Bellmore-Freeport area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore community and bay landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: The Merrick neck lands show how Native community life was organized around water, meadow, and bay access. A visitor looking south from Merrick or Bellmore is seeing a landscape that supported fishing, shellfishing, travel, planting, and kinship long before suburban roads and parcels.

rows.title: Merrick Preaching Visits, 1742
rows.summary: A Long Island Historical Journal article on Reverend Azariah Horton's 1742 mission journal records stops among Native groups at Merrick and neighboring places including Rockaway, Jerusalem/Wantagh, and Fort Neck. Horton's journal places Native people in the Merrick area generations after early colonial land transactions, showing continuity across western Long Island communities.
rows.address_label: Merrick area, Town of Hempstead
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as eighteenth-century evidence of Native presence in the Merrick area.
rows.why_this_matters: Horton's Merrick visits are evidence that Native people remained present and connected across western Long Island in the eighteenth century. The history challenges disappearance narratives and places Merrick within a living regional Native geography.

rows.title: Merrick Road: Ancient South Shore Trail
rows.summary: Local histories describe Merrick Road, once known as South Country Road, as following an older Indigenous footpath or forest trail across the south shore. The route linked waterways, settlements, planting areas, and neighboring communities before English road-building fixed it into the colonial landscape.
rows.address_label: Merrick Road / South Country Road corridor, Freeport-Baldwin-Merrick area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore travel corridor.
rows.why_this_matters: Merrick Road shows how everyday infrastructure can preserve traces of older Native geographies. Seen as a south shore travel corridor, the road carries histories of movement, exchange, and connection across Merrick ancestral land.

rows.title: Merrick Western Edge near Rockville Centre
rows.summary: Merrick community geography is described as extending west toward the Rockville Centre area, where Merrick, Rockaway, and other south shore Native histories met across waterways, meadows, and travel routes.
rows.address_label: Rockville Centre / western Merrick homeland edge
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a western-edge learning point for Merrick community geography.
rows.why_this_matters: The Rockville Centre edge of Merrick country shows how Native homelands crossed the lines later drawn by towns, villages, and roads. It also helps explain why Merrick, Rockaway, and Massapequa histories often appear together in colonial records and local memory.

rows.title: Merricks
rows.summary: Merrick territory is remembered across the southern part of Long Island, from the Rockville Centre area toward the western Oyster Bay line, with ties to necks, bays, and south-shore places. Older histories say the Merrick people moved east from the western end of Long Island into a landscape shaped by Massapequa power and tribute relationships. Those accounts are colonial-era interpretations; Merrick place names, community presence, and documented land relationships remain the focus here.

rows.title: Messemennuck (Peconic Bay)
rows.summary: Messemennuck is a Peconic Bay and river-boundary placename associated with alewife fishing and the western bounds of Shinnecock territory.

rows.title: Messtopass (Mannatto Hill)
rows.summary: Messtopass is documented as a boundary landmark near Mannatto Hill in the town of Oyster Bay. A Huntington place-name source places it on the western boundary south of Old Country Road.

rows.title: Miamegg (Jamesport Creek)
rows.summary: Miamegg is a Jamesport creek placename connected with a 1648 deed and interpreted as a meeting fishing-place.

rows.title: Mica Tablet Site
rows.summary: In 1849, New York State received a mica plate reportedly found while plowing in Brookhaven. Engraved geometric and other figures make the object unusual, but its exact findspot, age, and cultural interpretation remain uncertain.

rows.title: Milburn Creek and Bedell's Landing Vicinity
rows.summary: Milburn Creek and the Bedell's Landing area are part of a wider Freeport-Baldwin shoreline landscape where local histories remember Merrick maritime life, shellfishing, wampum-making materials, and stone implements found near the creek.
rows.address_label: Milburn Creek / Baldwin Bay vicinity, Baldwin-Freeport border
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Within and near Merrick ancestral land; connected to the broader creek-and-bay landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Milburn Creek connects Freeport-area waterways to Merrick shellfishing, wampum-making, travel, and coastal knowledge. The story belongs in a broad creek-and-bay landscape while respecting places that may still hold cultural materials.

rows.title: Minasseroke (Strong's Neck)
rows.summary: Minasseroke is connected with Little Neck, now Strong's Neck, at Setauket. The neck lies between Conscience Bay and Setauket Harbor and is associated in local history with Setalcott presence and a place remembered as Indian Ground.
rows.listing_image_alt: Strongs Neck Site Setauket, or Indian Ground Site_5I5A0316 WEB

rows.title: Minnahanonck (Roosevelt Island)
rows.summary: Minnahanonck is connected with Blackwell's Island in the East River, the island now known as Roosevelt Island. The name appears in early New Netherland sources connected with Marychtenwikingh people from present-day Brooklyn.

rows.title: Minnapaugs (Horton's Point Pond)
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker links Minnapaugs with a small freshwater pond by Long Island Sound at Horton's Point in Southold. The place also appears in Hashamomuk Neck boundary language, tying the pond to a wider named landscape west of Greenport.

rows.title: Minnesunk (North Sea Pond)
rows.summary: Minnesunk is a modern name applied to a pond at North Sea in Southampton, not an older Long Island Indigenous placename. It shows how later writers sometimes created Native-sounding names from mixed or imported language material.

rows.title: Minnisais (Liberty Island)
rows.summary: Minnisais is a Chippewa name applied by Henry R. Schoolcraft to Bedlow's Island, now Liberty Island. It is included here as a later introduced name, not an older local placename from Long Island or New York Harbor records.

rows.title: Mispatuck / Masquetux
rows.summary: A West Islip placename cluster linking Mispatuck, Mispotuck, Misputuck, Masquetux, neck land, brook geography, and older boundary language.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Missi Kesukut
rows.summary: Shinnecock advocates worked for decades to protect an archaeologically sensitive area in Water Mill from development. Their efforts shaped excavation safeguards, care for ancestral remains, and a later public preservation effort while keeping the exact sensitive location off the public map.
rows.address_label: Montauk Highway, Water Mill
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock intervention changed how Southampton Town handled archaeology, ancestral remains, and development in Water Mill. The history demonstrates that preservation depends on Native authority and sustained community advocacy, not only on what construction or excavation happens to uncover.

rows.title: Missing Meroke Village Marker, Merrick
rows.summary: A former New York State historic marker in Merrick acknowledged a Meroke village area. It is no longer standing, but its text keeps local memory of Meroke presence visible.
rows.address_label: Sunrise Highway vicinity, west of Central Boulevard, Merrick
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land through the former public marker and Meroke place history.
rows.why_this_matters: The missing Meroke marker shows how Native place history can be acknowledged in one generation and fade from the roadside landscape in another. Restoring the story helps reconnect Merrick to Meroke presence while treating village places with respect.

rows.title: Missipaug (Big Fresh Pond)
rows.summary: Missipaug is listed as a name suggested for Big Fresh Pond near North Sea. The name points to a real Southampton pond while also showing how some Native-sounding Long Island names were created or regularized by later writers.
rows.address_label: Big Fresh Pond, North Sea, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Mogkompskut (Great Rock)
rows.summary: Mogkompskut names a large boulder in the Hands Creek Road and Three Mile Harbor area of East Hampton. William Wallace Tooker preserved the name from Stephen Pharaoh of the Montaukett Tribe.
rows.address_label: Hands Creek Road near Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton, NY

rows.title: Molly's Hill
rows.summary: Molly's Hill is a remembered Montaukett place near the meeting of Fireplace Road and Gerard Drive in Springs. Jacqueline Overton's 1963 local history associates the hill with Molly Pharoah and the early life of her son, Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah. Later road construction altered the hill and its surrounding landscape.

rows.title: Momoweta Pond (Laurel Lake)
rows.summary: Momoweta Pond, now known as Laurel Lake, is a North Fork waterbody named for Momoweta, sachem of Corchaug.
rows.address_label: Laurel Lake, Laurel / Mattituck, Southold, NY

rows.title: Monabaugs (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Monabaugs names a creek, swamp, and pond in the Westhampton area between Potunk and Ketchaponack Necks. The history preserves a water-place name in a landscape where coastal wetlands and waterways have changed over time.
rows.address_label: Westhampton area between Potunk and Ketchaponack Necks, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Montaukett Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Montaukett Ancestral Land is the homeland of the Indigenous Montaukett people of eastern Long Island. Montaukett history connects the Montauk peninsula, neighboring Native communities, Algonquian language traditions, coastal knowledge, diplomacy, fishing and whaling, land defense and dispossession, survival, and continued community identity.
rows.listing_image_alt: 1879 public auction map of Montauk lands.
rows.why_this_matters: Montaukett Ancestral Land is a living homeland story, not only an East End place name. It connects language, fortified high land, shoreline movement, leadership, land loss, and continued Montaukett presence.

rows.title: Moriches
rows.summary: Moriches is a south-shore Brookhaven placename connected with a neck of land at Unquichoge and with the later hamlets of Moriches, Center Moriches, and East Moriches. Early forms include Merquices and Meritche.

rows.title: Mosquetah (Mosquito Cove)
rows.summary: Mosquetah is a Glen Cove placename remembered in the later English form Mosquito Cove. The name refers to meadows or rushes along the cove or creek, not to the insect.

rows.title: Munchog (Great Pond Island)
rows.summary: A Montauk island name in Great Pond, now Lake Montauk, connected with older forms such as Munchoage and Manchoage.

rows.title: Munnawtawkit (Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Munnawtawkit names Fishers Island, an island politically within Southold though closer to Connecticut. The name is connected with Pequot fishing and planting and with other eastern island and high-land names.

rows.title: Muskyttehool (Flatlands)
rows.summary: Muskyttehool is a Flatlands, Kings County placename for a pool or wet place where rushes grew. The popular Musquito hole explanation is best understood as a misunderstanding of a rush-place name.

rows.title: Musquatax / Squorums Neck
rows.summary: Musquatax names a creek on Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The cited source places it within Unkechaug land-title geography and interprets the name as a rush-growing place.

rows.title: Nachaquatuck (Cold Spring Harbor Creek)
rows.summary: Nachaquatuck names the creek or river at Cold Spring Harbor that marked Huntington's western boundary, linking the placename to boundary language and tidal-stream geography.

rows.title: Naghtognk (Corlears Hook)
rows.summary: A Manhattan placename for Corlears Hook, linked with Dutch forms Nechtauk and Nechtank and interpreted as a landmark-tree name.

rows.title: Nameoke (Rockaway)
rows.summary: Nameoke names a traditional locality near Rockaway village in old Hempstead town. The name is interpreted as a fishing-place name rather than a phrase meaning water edge.

rows.title: Nanemoset (Wading River Brook)
rows.summary: Nanemoset is an uncertain brook or creek placename associated with Quaconsit, now Wading River, or nearby fishing tributaries. The name is interpreted as at the fishing-place and is cross-referenced with the related Nemaukak form.

rows.title: Napock (Peconic River Headwaters)
rows.summary: Napock is connected with the Peconic River headwaters, a chain of ponds and wetlands along the Riverhead/Brookhaven boundary. The history preserves a boundary placename tied to water, pools, and the interior landscape of central Long Island. The name is interpreted as a water-place or pool-place.

rows.title: Narrioch (Gravesend Neck)
rows.summary: Narrioch is a Kings County placename associated with Gravesend Neck, interpreted as a point or corner of land. The name is tied to the same 1654 release that names Mannahanning.

rows.title: Nassakeag (South Setauket)
rows.summary: Nassakeag is connected with the southwest border of Setauket in Brookhaven town, in the locality later known as South Setauket. The name is tied both to a swamp and to Nassakeag, a Nissequogue sachem whose name appears in regional land records.

rows.title: Nayack (Fort Hamilton)
rows.summary: Nayack is connected with the New Utrecht point of land at present-day Fort Hamilton, directly opposite Staten Island. The history preserves a western Long Island shore name tied to the Narrows and the New Netherland period.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Nayantacawnick (Probable Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Nayantacawnick is the island name Roger Williams used in 1637 while discussing the forced placement of captive Pequot families. Historical place-name sources interpret it as being opposite Niantic and identify Fishers Island as the most likely modern location, while also naming Plum Island as an alternative.
rows.address_label: Fishers Island, Town of Southold, NY (probable broad identification)
rows.why_this_matters: Nayantacawnick preserves a seventeenth-century regional name while also documenting a proposal to confine Pequot families after war. Mapping the probable island makes that history visible, and retaining the uncertainty prevents a geographic inference from being presented as settled fact.

rows.title: Neapeague (Napeague Beach)
rows.summary: Neapeague, now commonly Napeague, is the sandy and marshy water-land connecting Montauk with the main part of Long Island in East Hampton town.

rows.title: Neckapauge (Green's Creek)
rows.summary: Neckapauge is associated with Green's Creek, west of Sayville in the Town of Islip. The name appears in connection with the eastern boundary and beginning bound of the Nicoll Patent.

rows.title: Neguntatogue (Lindenhurst)
rows.summary: Neguntatogue is associated with a neck of land south of Breslau, now Lindenhurst, between Little Neck and Santapogue.

rows.title: Nesaquaque Accompsett
rows.summary: The name is interpreted as land on the other side of Nissequogue, tying Smithtown west-river geography to Fresh Pond and older place-name records.

rows.title: Nesconset / Nasseconset
rows.summary: Nasseconset is connected with a Nissequogue sachem and with the modern hamlet name Nesconset in Smithtown. The name belongs to the Nissequogue River and Smithtown regional landscape, where personal names and land names often overlap in colonial records.

rows.title: Niamuck / Merosuck (Canoe Place)
rows.summary: Niamuck and Merosuck are recorded names connected with Canoe Place in Southampton, the narrow isthmus between Shinnecock Bay and Peconic Bay. The place is central to Shinnecock geography and to the portage route later cut by the Shinnecock Canal.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Canoe Place preserves the memory of an Indigenous portage route connecting two bays. Showing Niamuck and Merosuck together keeps both recorded names searchable while making clear that they describe the same broader landscape rather than two separate sites.

rows.title: Nippaug (Little Fresh Pond)
rows.summary: Nippaug is a later suggested Algonquian-style name for Little Fresh Pond, kept here with caution because the naming history differs from older local placename records.

rows.title: Nipscop (Conkling's Farm)
rows.summary: Nipscop is recorded as a traditional name for Conkling's Farm, a tract in the western part of Islip town and partly in Babylon. The history preserves a local name attached to a farm landscape whose exact modern bounds require review. The name's meaning remains uncertain.

rows.title: Nissequogue (Smithtown)
rows.summary: A Smithtown-area name preserved in Dutch and English forms, including Nisinckqueghacky and Nesequake.

rows.title: Nissequogue / Wissiquack River
rows.summary: Wissiquack is recorded as a corrupted form of Nissequogue in Smithtown and belongs with the Tackan/Nissequogue discussion.

rows.title: Nissequogue Ancestral Land
rows.summary: A North Shore homeland entry centered on Native presence, diplomacy, land pressure, and river-linked community memory.
rows.why_this_matters: Nissequogue Ancestral Land places the river and North Shore within Native geography. Place names, waterways, and boundary records carry evidence of Native presence, diplomacy, and land pressure across generations.

rows.title: Nobbs (Goose Creek)
rows.summary: Nobbs is a Flanders-area placename associated with Goose Creek, one of the creeks named in Paucamp's testimony about the west end of Peconic Bay.

rows.title: Noccomack (West Mastic Meadows)
rows.summary: Noccomack is connected with meadows and land on the west side of Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The recorded forms point to a wetland place between upland and bay on the Mastic Peninsula.

rows.title: Nominick Hills
rows.summary: Nominick is connected with hills on Montauk in East Hampton, where the high land rises out of the sandy and marshy Neapeague. The placename is remembered through traditional usage and later local writing rather than early town records.

rows.title: Nonowantuck (Crystal Brook)
rows.summary: Nonowantuck is connected with Mount Sinai in Brookhaven. The placename refers to a small stream that once ran from the interior plains toward the west side of Mount Sinai Harbor, leaving a valley later known as Crystal Brook.

rows.title: North Merrick Descendant Community Landscape
rows.summary: Source research identifies North Merrick within a broader descendant-community landscape where Native families and related kin networks remained after land loss through survivance, intermarriage, labor, landholding, and community memory.
rows.address_label: North Merrick area, Town of Hempstead
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a Native descendant-community learning point.
rows.why_this_matters: North Merrick's Native descendant history shows that Merrick survivance continued through family networks, adaptation, labor, landholding, and community memory. The neighborhood is presented as a broad landscape of Native continuity after land loss.

rows.title: North Neck Burial Ground Rally
rows.summary: The North Neck Burial Ground Rally brought Montaukett families, Shinnecock supporters, singers, and allies together to defend an eighteenth-century Montaukett burial ground connected with Cyrus Charles.
rows.address_label: North Neck, Montauk (generalized)
rows.why_this_matters: This stop shows intercommunity support and public ceremony as part of burial-ground defense.

rows.title: Nowedonah (Lake Nowedonah / Mill Pond)
rows.summary: Nowedonah is the name of a Shinnecock sachem and was later given to Mill Pond at Water Mill. The placename preserves a connection between the Water Mill pond and Shinnecock leadership remembered in seventeenth-century records.

rows.title: Noyack (Jessup's Neck)
rows.summary: Noyack is associated with Noyack Bay, the hamlet now often spelled Noyac, and the long point or neck of land known as Jessup's Neck. The area also has archaeological evidence of long Indigenous use, including village and procurement-site contexts around Noyack.

rows.title: Opcatkontycke Creek
rows.summary: Opcatkontycke names a brook at Northport in Huntington. The name appears in the first Huntington purchase, where the stream formed the eastern boundary of the tract opposite Nachaquetack at Cold Spring Harbor.

rows.title: Orient Burial
rows.summary: The Orient Site is one of four known Orient Period (1,300 - 1,000 BC) burials on eastern Long Island. The cultural period receives its name from the fish shaped projectile points with distinct shoulders. During this period, the areas used for ceremonial burials were greatly removed from habitation areas, suggesting a reverence for their preservation. Oral stories support this hypothesis.
rows.address_label: Main Road, Orient area

rows.title: Osprey Road Burial Site Confrontation
rows.summary: After construction exposed a Native group burial on Shelter Island in October 2003, Shinnecock community members pressed town officials for respect, consultation, and stronger protection of ancestral remains. The confrontation became part of a broader effort to improve burial-protection law.
rows.address_label: Shelter Island Town Board, Shelter Island (site generalized)
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock advocates turned the disturbance of ancestors into a public demand for consultation, respect, and stronger burial-protection law.

rows.title: Ouheywichkingh (Unkechaug village)
rows.summary: Ouheywichkingh is a Dutch-recorded form for an Unkechaug village near Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The name belongs with the wider Unkechaug place-name record, but it is preserved here because the 1645 treaty form is distinct and historically important.

rows.title: Pagganck / Governors Island
rows.summary: Pagganck is the name recorded for modern Governors Island in a June 16, 1637 deed. The record names Cacapeteyno and Pewihas as owners acting with the consent of their community at Keshaechquereren and conveys the island to Wouter van Twiller. Later sources also preserve the spelling Pagganch.
rows.address_label: Governors Island, New York Harbor, New York, NY (historic northern island footprint)

rows.title: Pantigo
rows.summary: Pantigo names a locality between East Hampton village and Amagansett. The place is also associated with Pantigo Hill, where a seventeenth-century Montaukett cemetery was documented in the early twentieth century.

rows.title: Papequatunck
rows.summary: Papequatunck is an Oyster Bay placename from a 1653 deed, interpreted as opened or broken-up land and associated with Native planting ground west of Oyster Bay River. Papequatunck is an Oyster Bay placename preserved in the first Indian deed for Oyster Bay. The name marks the western side of the land description and is associated with land cleared for Native planting.

rows.title: Paquatuck (Terrell River)
rows.summary: Paquatuck names the creek or tidal river now known as Terrell River, on the line between East Moriches and Center Moriches in Brookhaven. The name appears in colonial boundary language for Moriches Neck.

rows.title: Pascu-ucks
rows.summary: Pascu-ucks is connected with a creek on the island historically called Screcunkas, now associated with Cedar Island in Babylon's Great South Bay.

rows.title: Passasqueung / Arrasquaug
rows.summary: Passasqueung and Arrasquaug are connected with a creek at South Oyster Bay, now associated in the source with Minell's Creek.

rows.title: Passquessit (East End of Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Passquessit is a placename for the east end of Fishers Island, an adjacent island in the Town of Southold.

rows.title: Patchogue
rows.summary: Patchogue is a Brookhaven placename connected with Pochoug Neck, local stream geography, and later village history on the south shore of Long Island.

rows.title: Patchummuck (Tom's Creek)
rows.summary: Patchummuck is connected with a boundary point at the head of Tom's Creek on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold.

rows.title: Pattersquash Island
rows.summary: A Mastic Neck place name in Unkechaug homelands tied to island, creek, meadow, and tract names in the Pattersquas landscape.

rows.title: Patuckquapaug
rows.summary: Patuckquapaug, located on the edge of what is now known as Round Pond in Sag Harbor, was once a village site for what was likely a subgroup of the Shinnecock.

rows.title: Paucuckatux (Tom's Creek)
rows.summary: Paucuckatux is identified as a creek on the bounds of Hashamomuk Neck in Southold, probably the stream known as Tom's Creek.

rows.title: Paumanack / Eastern Long Island
rows.summary: Paumanack is a broad Indigenous placename documented for Eastern Long Island, not a single village, creek, neck, or pond. Its marker is a representative regional label rather than a boundary.
rows.address_label: Eastern Long Island (representative map label near Riverhead / Peconic)
rows.why_this_matters: Paumanack names Eastern Long Island at a regional scale and keeps Indigenous political and geographic relationships visible beyond modern town boundaries. The representative marker invites visitors to read the linked records without reducing a broad homeland to one exact coordinate.

rows.title: Pauquacumsuck / Pahquahkossit (Wading River)
rows.summary: Pauquacumsuck, also recorded as Pahquahkossit and related forms, is the Wading River creek placename tied to the Occabuck boundary and clam-wading interpretation.

rows.title: Payaquotusk (Pipe's Neck)
rows.summary: Payaquotusk is a Southold placename for Pipe's Neck in the Arshamomaque and Hashamomuk Neck landscape.

rows.title: Peacepunck (West Branch of Nissequogue River)
rows.summary: Peacepunck names the west branch of the Nissequogue River in Smithtown, where a partition division among Richard Smith's heirs described a branch south of the mills.

rows.title: Peconic
rows.summary: Peconic is a long-running eastern Long Island placename now associated with the Peconic River, Peconic Bay, and the hamlet of Peconic.

rows.title: Pell Site
rows.summary: In 1997, the Pell case began, involving an attempt to steal Shinnecock Reservation land. On a strip of land south of Montauk Highway and the Tide Water Pub, the Shinnecock tribe successfully defended the land from being taken and developed.

rows.title: Penataquit Creek (Bay Shore)
rows.summary: Penataquit is a Bay Shore placename associated with Penataquit Creek and with older boundary language for Aweeksa Neck in Islip.

rows.title: Pequash (Goldsmith's Neck)
rows.summary: Pequash is a Cutchogue placename for a neck of land known as Goldsmith's Neck, interpreted as open or cleared ground.

rows.title: Pesapunck
rows.summary: Pesapunck is a Southold placename for a neck and meadow between Cutchogue and Mattituck, interpreted as a hot house or sweat lodge place.

rows.title: Pomiches Creek (East Moriches)
rows.summary: Pomiches is an East Moriches creek placename remembered as the western boundary of Watchogue Neck and interpreted as a crossing or crossway.

rows.title: Ponquogue / Bondyquogue
rows.summary: Ponquogue is represented as a Hampton Bays placename with Bondyquogue kept as a related spelling or cross-reference form. The blue marker gives a modern orientation near Ponquogue Bridge.

rows.title: Poquatuck (Orient Point / Long Beach Bay)
rows.summary: Poquatuck is an Orient Point and Long Beach Bay placename in Southold, interpreted as a clear or open tidal cove or creek.

rows.title: Poquott (Dyer's Neck)
rows.summary: Poquott is a traditional placename for Dyer's Neck between Setauket and Port Jefferson, interpreted as clear land or open country but treated cautiously by Tooker.

rows.title: Potinack
rows.summary: Potinack is a Montauk placename for a hole or deep depression in the Hither Plains and Hither Woods landscape, with related watering-place references at Montauk and Amagansett.
rows.listing_image_alt: Potinack, Napeague Bay archaeological landscape and corn fields
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Potunk Neck (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Potunk is a Westhampton placename for Potunk Neck and nearby meadowland, recorded in seventeenth-century Southampton and East Hampton references and interpreted as a boggy place.

rows.title: Poyhas Swamp
rows.summary: Poyhas is recorded as a swamp within the Hashamomuk bounds in Southold. The place is connected with Poyhas, a Native person who lived and planted there.

rows.title: Preservation Long Island
rows.summary: Preservation Long Island worked with Indigenous artists and guest curators to present Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place in 2020. The online exhibition brought contemporary Native art into conversation with Long Island land, water, wildlife, history, and community.
rows.address_label: 161 West Main Street, Cold Spring Harbor, NY 11724
rows.listing_image_alt: Artwork from Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place, shared by Preservation Long Island.
rows.why_this_matters: References: Preservation Long Island, "Virtual Exhibition: Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place," July 31, 2020, preservationlongisland.org; Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place, About, indigenoushistoryandart.omeka.net.

rows.title: Pumcatawe
rows.summary: Pumcatawe is recorded as a small tract of land and meadow east of Mastic River in Brookhaven. The name is connected with a Native person who formerly lived on the land.

rows.title: Pung-Plues Creek
rows.summary: Pung-Plues is recorded as a small creek at Moriches in Brookhaven. In a 1681 deed, it formed the western boundary of a small neck of land and meadow near Watchogue and the bay.

rows.title: Punk's Hole (Manorville)
rows.summary: Punk's Hole was a former name for the village known as Manor, now associated with Manorville, or for a nearby hollow. The name combines a local hollow with punk, an Algonquian word used for fungus or tinder from old oak trees and stumps.

rows.title: Quadams Hill
rows.summary: Quadams is recorded as a hill in the Indian Field near Oyster Pond at Montauk. The name appears to preserve a personal name attached to a feature in the Montaukett landscape.

rows.title: Quagga Path
rows.summary: Quagga, also written Quogo or Quago, is recorded as an Indian trail or path in western Southampton at Atlanticville, now the East Quogue area. The name was used for a path leading toward Quaquanantuck Neck and the meadows.

rows.title: Qualican
rows.summary: Qualican is recorded as a locality on Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The name appears in the 1700 William Smith deed connected with lands for the Unkechaug people at Pusspatok.

rows.title: Quanch Island
rows.summary: Quanch is recorded as an island in Great South Bay opposite Bellport in Brookhaven. The name appears in a town-record description involving meadowland and Whale House Point.

rows.title: Quandoequareous (Newtown Creek)
rows.summary: A Queens creek-name for the west branch of Newtown Creek, connected in older records with the Mespat kills.

rows.title: Quanuntowunk (Fort Pond)
rows.summary: A Montauk deed placename pairing Fort Pond geography with Konkhunganik and showing how north and south pond-side places were recorded together.

rows.title: Quaquanantuck / Quantuck Bay and Creek
rows.summary: A western Southampton creek, bay, meadow, and purchase-record name preserved in seventeenth-century sources.

rows.title: Quarapin (Round Swamp)
rows.summary: A Huntington swamp placename remembered as the planting place of a Native person named Quarapin.

rows.title: Quggalune
rows.summary: Quggalune is recorded as a locality in western Southampton, in the Quoquanantuck or Quogue purchase landscape near Assop's Neck.

rows.title: Quiogue
rows.summary: Quiogue is recorded as a neck of land between Aspatuck and Quantuck creeks in western Southampton. The place was formerly known as Little Assop's Neck.

rows.title: Quogue
rows.summary: Quogue is recorded as a village in western Southampton on Quantuck Bay. The name is a shortened form of Quaquanantuck, the older name for the salt meadows and land in this section.

rows.title: Quonettquott
rows.summary: Quonettquott is connected with the West Connecticut River, known as Connetquot Brook in Islip. The name is interpreted as at the long river.

rows.title: Raconkamuck / Lake Ronkonkoma
rows.summary: Raconkamuck, now Lake Ronkonkoma, is a central Long Island freshwater lake on the bounds of Brookhaven, Islip, and Smithtown. The name is interpreted as a boundary or fence fishing-place.

rows.title: Rapahamuck
rows.summary: Rapahamuck appears in western Southampton records around Flanders, Birch Creek, and the Aquebaug meadow allotments. The name is tied to a neck, point, and island, so the map marker is best understood as a general landscape reference rather than one exact point.

rows.title: Rassapeague
rows.summary: A Stony Brook Harbor swamp, meadow, and bay placename interpreted as a muddy or miry water place.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Reeve Farm Site
rows.summary: The Reeve Farm Site is remembered through the disturbance, collection, and public display of Native ancestral remains uncovered in Aquebogue in 1961. The episode shows how farming, collecting, archaeological interpretation, and museum display harmed Native ancestors and why burial protection remains necessary.

rows.title: Rev. Paul Cuffee Gravesite
rows.summary: A single fenced grave marks the burial location of Reverend Paul Cuffee, a Shinnecock minister connected with the old Native church meeting place at Good Ground, now Hampton Bays. Cuffee followed the religious path of his grandfather Peter John and preached among Native communities on Long Island.
rows.address_label: Good Ground Road area

rows.title: Rinnegackonck
rows.summary: Rinnegackonck is a Brooklyn placename associated with the plantation of George Rapaljee and early Dutch records near western Long Island.

rows.title: Roanoke Point
rows.summary: Roanoke is recorded as a point of land on the north shore of Long Island in Riverhead town. The source cautions that it was probably adopted from Roanoke in Virginia rather than being an original Long Island Indigenous name.

rows.title: Rockaway
rows.summary: Rockaway is a place-name associated with the Rockaway Peninsula and the Rockaway people. The name is recorded in seventeenth-century deeds and is interpreted as referring to sandy land or country.

rows.title: Rockaway Traditional Land
rows.summary: Rockaway and Reckouwacky names belong to a coastal world of villages, bays, islands, travel routes, diplomacy, and land records across western Long Island and present-day Brooklyn/Queens. The territory is remembered alongside neighboring Merrick and Canarsie landscapes, not as an isolated place.
rows.why_this_matters: Rockaway Traditional Land presents western Long Island, Jamaica Bay, Hempstead Bay, and the south shore islands as Native homeland. It connects early records with waterways, coastal movement, and the continued importance of public memory.

rows.title: Rockaway and the Southern Hempstead Bays
rows.summary: Rockaway people are described in older histories with a principal settlement near what is now Rockville Centre, with others spread through southern Hempstead and islands in the bays along the south shore. This places Native life around the waterways west of Merrick and Freeport as part of a connected regional world.
rows.address_label: Southern Hempstead bay landscape near Rockville Centre and Freeport
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Associated with Merrick Ancestral Land at its western edge, while also recognizing neighboring Rockaway Native geography.
rows.why_this_matters: The Rockaway and southern Hempstead bay landscape places Merrick history in relation to neighboring Native communities. Bays, islands, and waterways connected people across homelands before colonial town borders divided the map.

rows.title: Ronkonkoma Moraine
rows.summary: Unkechaug, a name for the nation of Indigenous peoples living in Mastic, New York, translates to "people from beyond the hill." Today, these hills are part of the Ronkonkoma Moraine, a chain of hills that span the center of Long Island. The Unkechaug Nations territory once ran along the south of the Ronkonkoma Moraine.
rows.why_this_matters: The Ronkonkoma Moraine gives landscape context for the Unkechaug name and homeland. Donna Barron records Unkechaug as "People from Beyond the Hill," while John A. Strong places Unkechaug villages in the southern half of Brookhaven when Europeans arrived in the mid-seventeenth century. References: Donna Barron, The Long Island Indians and Their New England Ancestors; John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011).

rows.title: Rugs
rows.summary: Rugs is recorded as a Southampton Town place-name at Noyack, connected with a neck of land and creek. The stream is associated with Thompson's Trout Ponds.
rows.address_label: General area of Trout Pond / Thompson's Trout Ponds, Noyack, Southampton Town

rows.title: Rugua Swamp
rows.summary: Rugua is recorded as a swamp in the Town of Babylon near Copiag Neck.

rows.title: Ruscocunks Creek
rows.summary: Ruscocunks is recorded as a creek east of Mastic Neck in the Town of Brookhaven.

rows.title: Ruskatux (Seaman's Neck)
rows.summary: A Seaford / Seaman's Neck placename for meadows and uplands east of an earlier Indian purchase.

rows.title: Sachem's Hole
rows.summary: Sachem's Hole, also known as Whooping Boy's Hollow and Buc-usk-kil, marks a resting place remembered in accounts of Poggatacut's funeral procession from Shelter Island toward Montauk.

rows.title: Sachem's House
rows.summary: Sachem's House connects a 1650 Southampton record with Shinnecock leadership and the way colonial documents sometimes preserved Native political places.

rows.title: Sachem's Neck
rows.summary: A Shelter Island placename connected to Native leadership, family movement, and Mashomuck history.

rows.title: Sackhickneyah Creek
rows.summary: Sackhickneyah is recorded as a creek in northern Newtown, Queens County, near Fish's Point.

rows.title: Sacut (Success Pond)
rows.summary: Sacut is recorded as the Native name for Success Pond at Lakeville in North Hempstead.

rows.title: Sagamore Hill
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker includes Sagamore Hill at Oyster Bay, recording Theodore Roosevelt's explanation that the name was a revival connected with local traditions about Mohannis Cove and Mohannis Hill.

rows.title: Sagaponack / Sagg Pond
rows.summary: Sagaponack is an eastern Southampton place-name also preserved in Sagg, Sagg Pond, and Sag Harbor. The name is connected with ground-nuts or Indian potatoes.

rows.title: Saghtekoos / Appletree Neck
rows.summary: Saghtekoos is recorded as a neck of land in Islip, known in English records as Appletree Neck.

rows.title: Santapogue Neck
rows.summary: Santapogue is recorded as a neck of land in Babylon, south of the settlement of Breslau, now Lindenhurst.

rows.title: Saphorackam
rows.summary: Saphorackam is recorded as a locality in southern Brooklyn, near the Long Island strand of the North River bay.

rows.title: Sassian's Maize Land
rows.summary: Sassians was a Brooklyn locality named in a 1642 Kieft grant as Sassian's maize land.

rows.title: Saugust Neck (Southold Old Field)
rows.summary: Saugust is recorded as a neck of land at the east part of Southold.

rows.title: Scoquams Creek / Schookwames Neck
rows.summary: Scoquams is recorded as a neck of land and small creek in Islip, east of Babylon village.

rows.title: Screcunkas (Cedar Island)
rows.summary: Screcunkas is recorded as an island in Great South Bay, now known as Cedar Island in Babylon.

rows.title: Scurraway / Josiah's Neck
rows.summary: Scurraway is recorded as the Native name of Josiah's Neck in Babylon, east of Amityville.

rows.title: Seabamuck / Sebamuck
rows.summary: Seabamuck is recorded as one of the lesser necks of the Manor of St. George at Mastic, first east of the Connecticut or Carmans River at its mouth.

rows.title: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck Cultural Landscape
rows.summary: A south shore estuarine landscape tied to Native village life, shellfishing, fishing, bay travel, and coastal resource use in Merrick and Massapequa homelands.
rows.address_label: Seaford Creek / Unqua Neck waterways, Seaford-Massapequa area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Within the wider Merrick/Massapequa south shore cultural landscape; linked here to Merrick Ancestral Land with care about overlapping homelands.
rows.why_this_matters: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck show why tidal waterways and neck lands mattered: they were living landscapes, travel routes, and foodways rather than empty marshes.

rows.title: Seapoose (Meacox Bay Inlet)
rows.summary: Seapoose names inlets opened through the south-side beaches of East Hampton and Southampton, especially the inlet between Meacox Bay and the ocean.

rows.title: Seatquaa: Creek-Mouth Wetland Place Name
rows.summary: Seatquaa is a place-name connected with land at the mouth of a creek or tidal stream. The name helps explain how Native geographic language described estuaries, creek mouths, marshes, and movement through the south shore.
rows.address_label: South shore creek-mouth landscape, Freeport-Merrick-Bellmore area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore wetland/place-name learning point.
rows.why_this_matters: Seatquaa presents the south shore as Native geography: creek mouths, marshes, and bay edges were named and meaningful places for fishing, shellfishing, travel, and settlement. The word opens a way to understand wetlands as cultural landscapes.

rows.title: Seatuck Creek
rows.summary: Seatuck is a creek or river at Eastport on the boundary between Southampton and Brookhaven.

rows.title: Seawanhacky / Sewanhaka
rows.summary: Seawanhacky, also Sewanhaka, is a name for Long Island found in Dutch-period purchase documents.

rows.title: Sebonac Creek Settlement / Seponack
rows.summary: Seponack, also Sabonac, is recorded as a neck of land at Southampton on Peconic Bay. The name also connects the related Sebonac Creek Settlement and the Sabonack cross-reference.

rows.title: Secatogue Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Secatogue homelands are remembered along Great South Bay, east of Massapequa, across tidal creeks, neck lands, inland routes, and south shore villages. Records connect the name with Secatogue country and with neighboring Massapequa, Merrick, Setauket, and central Long Island Native histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Secatogue Ancestral Land presents Great South Bay creeks, marshes, and inland routes as Native geography. It also connects older records to descendant community memory and the continued presence of Native families on Long Island.

rows.title: Secatogue Neck
rows.summary: Secatogue is recorded as a neck of land in Islip and the locality associated with the Secatogue people.

rows.title: Secatogues
rows.summary: Secatogue is used in older sources for a south-shore Native community and place-name region east of Massapequa. Its history belongs with tidal creeks, Great South Bay travel, fishing and shellfish places, kinship, neighboring communities, regional diplomacy, and colonial land pressure.

rows.title: Senex Creek / Senekes River
rows.summary: Senex is recorded as a creek at Center Moriches, also called Senekes River or Creek.

rows.title: Setalcott Powwow Grounds
rows.summary: The Setalcott Powwow and Annual Corn Festival are held every July 11th at the Setauket Elementary School. The goal of the event is to educate the public about Setalcott family history and culture, as well as recognizing the continued presence of local tribal members. The Powwow was founded by Theodore Green in 2005, who had been chief of the Setalcott at the time, and later passed in 2007.
rows.listing_image_alt: Setaukett Setalcott Powwow Grounds School5I5A0306 WEB

rows.title: Setauket Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Setauket and Setalcott homelands connect north-central Long Island shorelines, villages, deeds, descendant community memory, and contemporary cultural education.
rows.why_this_matters: Setauket Ancestral Land presents the north-central shore as Native homeland, not only as colonial-settlement history. It connects language, villages, land records, descendant community memory, and contemporary cultural education.

rows.title: Shagwong Point, Hill, and Reef
rows.summary: Shagwong is a Montauk placename for a hill, point of land, and reef on the northeastern part of the peninsula, within the Indian Fields area.

rows.title: Shahchippitchage Boundary Stones
rows.summary: Shahchippitchage is a Montauk boundary-mark name for a pile of stones in North Neck, in the land between Fort Pond and Lake Montauk.

rows.title: Shanscomacocke (Flatlands)
rows.summary: Shanscomacocke is a Kings County placename at Flatlands, associated with enclosed upland, marsh, and beach land near the ocean.

rows.title: Sherawoug (Stony Brook Harbor)
rows.summary: Sherawoug is recorded as a locality on the east side of Stony Brook Harbor, near St. James in Smithtown.

rows.title: Shinnecock (Neck, Bay, Hills, and Plain)
rows.summary: Shinnecock is a major eastern Long Island placename associated with the Shinnecock people, Shinnecock plain, Shinnecock Hills, Shinnecock Bay, and the reservation.

rows.title: Shinnecock Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Shinnecock Ancestral Land gathers Southampton-area homelands, sacred and coastal places, land records, cultural continuity, and present-day sovereignty.
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock Ancestral Land presents Southampton and the South Fork as the homeland of a living Native nation. It connects early records, Native leadership, land protection, cultural continuity, and present-day Shinnecock sovereignty.

rows.title: Shinnecock Hills
rows.summary: Shinnecock Hills is sacred Shinnecock land and a burial landscape with ancestors present for thousands of years. The hills also sit at the center of later land-loss history, preservation fights, and public disputes over development, golf, and recognition of Shinnecock land rights.
rows.address_label: Sunrise Highway / Shinnecock Territory, Southampton
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club
rows.summary: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club sits within the broader Shinnecock Hills landscape, part of Shinnecock ancestral territory and the land at the center of the 1703 lease and 1859 land-loss history. The course is also a place where Shinnecock labor, caddying, greenskeeping, and golf history are visible, including Oscar Bunn and generations of Shinnecock workers. The 2026 U.S. Open brings global attention back to this landscape, making source-grounded land acknowledgment especially important.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club, Southampton, NY (general public course area)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shinnecock Hills is documented in Shinnecock land-history sources as part of the lands covered by the 1703 lease and later 1859 land-loss dispute. The marker gives broad course-area context rather than a burial or other sensitive-site coordinate.
rows.why_this_matters: The 2026 U.S. Open landscape is Shinnecock homeland, not only a famous golf course. It connects championship history to land loss, burial-ground disruption, and Shinnecock labor and skill: tribal members helped build and maintain the course, Oscar Bunn played in the 1896 U.S. Open, and later Shinnecock workers shaped the grounds across generations.

rows.title: Shinnecock Indian Reservation
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Reservation is a continuing Shinnecock homeland and center of Shinnecock government, culture, family life, education, worship, art, shellfish restoration, and community gathering. More than a historic district, it is a living Native nation space tied to Shinnecock land defense, the annual powwow, cultural preservation, and ongoing sovereignty.
rows.address_label: 1 Church St, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Monument
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Monument is an economic development project launched in early May 2019. The Shinnecock Nation's goal with this project is to generate revenue to provide for its people. Being a sovereign nation, The Shinnecock Nation maintains the right to build on its land and pursue commerce free from civil regulatory restrictions improperly imposed by New York State.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum is a Shinnecock-owned and operated museum dedicated to Shinnecock and Eastern Woodland history, culture, art, and living community memory. The museum preserves and interprets materials connected to Shinnecock life while challenging older museum habits that treated Native people as figures of the past.

rows.title: Shinnecock Outpost Tax Demonstrations
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Outpost became a public assertion of Shinnecock sovereignty during 1997 organizing against renewed state tax pressure.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Indian Outpost, 42 Montauk Highway, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.why_this_matters: This stop connects local Shinnecock action to wider Native coalitions across New York.

rows.title: Shinnecock Oyster Project
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Oyster Project connects Shinnecock maritime knowledge, shellfish restoration, aquaculture training, environmental stewardship, and living Native continuity in Shinnecock Bay.

rows.title: Shinnecock Powwow Grounds
rows.summary: Formally organized in 1946, the Shinnecock Powwow is a decades long traditional and cultural celebration that takes place on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation. Every year on Labor Day weekend, the Powwow takes place on Shinnecock and is open to the public. The annual four-day Shinnecock Labor Day Powwow attracts more than 15,000 attendees each day and serves as both a cultural focal point and fundraiser for the Nation. The Powwow began as historical 'pageants' that took place throughout Southampton Town,.
rows.activity_pin_preview: The Shinnecock Nation hosts the 80th Annual Shinnecock Powwow on Labor Day Weekend, September 4-7, 2026, at the Shinnecock Powwow Grounds, 100 Montauk Hwy, Southampton. Source: Shinnecock Nation annual powwow page.

rows.title: Shinnecock Presbyterian Church
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Presbyterian church on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation has been described as “the oldest, ongoing Native American church in America.” A regular schedule of tribal gatherings occur here, including the annual June Meeting, Indian Thanksgiving dinner and harvest celebrations. For many years, tribal meetings and Tribal Council elections were held in the Parish Hall before taking place in the Tribal Community Center. The Shinnecock Powwow was first organized by the Presbyterian church congregation as a.

rows.title: Shockheyoune
rows.summary: Shockheyoune appears in deed language for a swamp and creek at the Nissequogue River mouth. Its location on the west side of the river connects the name to shoreline, wetland, and boundary records along Long Island Sound.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Nissequogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Sintsinck (Manhasset Bay)
rows.summary: Sintsinck was recorded for Manhasset Bay or a locality on the bay at Cow Neck, with a separate related use recorded near Hell Gate Neck in Queens.

rows.title: Skow Island (South Oyster Bay)
rows.summary: Skow Island is a tidal marsh island in South Oyster Bay. Tooker recorded Skow as an early-map spelling associated with the island; modern federal maps preserve the island at this exact location under an outdated historical name.
rows.address_label: South Oyster Bay marsh island, Nassau County, NY
rows.why_this_matters: The island is a clearly identifiable part of the South Oyster Bay marsh landscape. Mapping it with careful language allows the archive to preserve a historical place-name record without repeating outdated terminology as an unqualified public label.

rows.title: Skupash Creek (Jamaica Meadows)
rows.summary: A Jamaica Meadows creek name recorded in a 1657 division of meadow lots.

rows.title: Slongo / Sunken Meadow
rows.summary: Slongo is a recorded name associated with Sunk Meadow, now Sunken Meadow, in Smithtown. Its location is clear, but its linguistic origin remains unresolved and may not be Indigenous.
rows.address_label: Sunken Meadow State Park, Kings Park, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Slongo is useful precisely because the map can separate a confident location from an uncertain origin. Publishing the record with that distinction prevents a historical name from being presented as confirmed Indigenous language when the available sources do not establish that conclusion.

rows.title: Sonquoequahesick / Sonnquoquas
rows.summary: Sonquoequahesick, also Sonnquoquas, is associated with Sonquoqua and Tom's Creek on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: South Harbor
rows.summary: South Harbor appears in Southold records during a period of increasing pressure on Corchaug land. Town records set aside about 120 acres there in 1685, but a 1763 Native petition disputed later claims that the community had settled at South Harbor and stated that descendants had lived at Indian Neck since 1691.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: South Ocean Gallery at South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation
rows.summary: South Ocean Gallery at South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation in Freeport is the venue for Living Conduit - Indigenous History and Present Day, a fall 2026 exhibition by Shinnecock artist Jeremy Dennis.
rows.address_label: 228 South Ocean Avenue, Freeport, NY 11520
rows.why_this_matters: This Freeport venue is part of the modern acknowledgment landscape for Merrick/Freeport-area Indigenous history. The 2026 Living Conduit exhibition connects On This Site place research with contemporary Shinnecock portraiture, education, and continuing Long Island Indigenous presence.

rows.title: Southold Indian Museum
rows.summary: The Southold Indian Museum opened in 1962 with a mission to study surrounding archaeology and natural history. It is owned and operated by the Incorporated Long Island Chapter of the New York State Archaeological Association. In 1990, the museum was forced to remove human remains that were on display through the efforts of Shinnecock tribal member David Bunn Martine and local Professor of history John A. Strong. In more recent years, the museum has worked towards repatriating human remains that had been in their.
rows.address_label: 1080 Main Bayview Rd, Southold, NY 11971
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Souwassett (Port Jefferson)
rows.summary: Souwassett is a locality at Port Jefferson in Brookhaven, connected with the earlier English name Drowned Meadow.

rows.title: Speonk (Neck, River, and Village)
rows.summary: Speonk is a village in western Southampton, originally named for a neck of land, with Speonk River on the east.

rows.title: Springy Banks Pow Wow Grounds
rows.summary: Springy Banks at Three Mile Harbor became an intertribal gathering place for powwows in 1944 and 1945, with later gatherings continuing into the early 1950s. Montaukett, Shinnecock, Matinecock, Narragansett, Schaghticoke, Cherokee, and other Native participants met there.
rows.address_label: Springy Banks / Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton (generalized)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Springy Banks gatherings show Native people building regional relationships during the mid-twentieth century, when public histories often spoke of Long Island's Indigenous communities only in the past. The powwows affirmed community, diplomacy, and continuing Native presence.

rows.title: Squam-Pit Purchase
rows.summary: Squam-Pit is recorded as a tract near Deer Park, now in the Wyandanch area, historically within Huntington.

rows.title: Squassux Landing / Squassucks Point
rows.summary: Squassux Landing / Squassucks Point is a Carmans River mouth placename tied to Unkechaug history, clay beds, pottery, ferry landings, and local memory at Brookhaven.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: St. Matthew Chapel
rows.summary: St. Matthew Chapel is one of the surviving buildings associated with Freetown, an East Hampton neighborhood shaped by Black and Montaukett families. Built in 1852, the chapel served local worshippers before it was moved to the Maidstone Marina boatyard in 1976.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah House
rows.summary: The Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah house was used by Pharoah later in his life. The house featured two "Indian barns" as food storage, and a footpath toward Bridgehampton on it's edge. The foundation remains today, but the house may have been a wood cabin during its use.
rows.address_label: Old Tar Road area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Stony Brook Site
rows.summary: The Stony Brook Site is an archaeological site in Stony Brook, New York, connected with Archaic-period Native occupation near the North Shore area of Aunt Amy's Creek. Excavations by William A. Ritchie and later archaeologists helped document long Indigenous presence, toolmaking, shellfish use, and the need to protect archaeological places from disturbance.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Sucos (Brookville)
rows.summary: Sucos is recorded as the site of Brookville in Oyster Bay, historically remembered as Suco's wigwam.

rows.title: Sugar Loaf Hill
rows.summary: Sugar Loaf Hill is tied to Orient-period burial context in the Shinnecock Hills and decades of Shinnecock advocacy for burial protection. Historic maps and later preservation efforts show how burial landscapes have been marked, damaged, contested, and defended.
rows.address_label: Montauk Highway corridor
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Suggamuck (Birch Creek)
rows.summary: Suggamuck is recorded as a creek near Flanders, now called Birch Creek, one of the creeks at the west end of Peconic Bay.

rows.title: Sumpawams Creek and Neck
rows.summary: Sumpawams is a Babylon-area name now applied to the creek between Babylon and Islip, originally belonging to the neck where much of Babylon village stands.

rows.title: Sungic (Shelter Island)
rows.summary: Sungic is a point of land and creek on the east side of Shelter Island, facing Gardiners Bay.

rows.title: Sunkapogue Creek (Mastic Neck)
rows.summary: Sunkapogue is a creek in Brookhaven on Mastic Neck, connected with the east bounds of a half-neck of land.

rows.title: Sunwicks Creek (Astoria)
rows.summary: Sunwicks is a creek at Astoria in Queens, near Hell Gate on Long Island.

rows.title: Swego / Centerport
rows.summary: Swego is a Huntington locality recorded in a 1771 town order. A Town of Huntington historical marker identifies the name with this Centerport area on Fort Salonga Road.
rows.address_label: Fort Salonga Road near Stony Hollow Road, Centerport, NY
rows.why_this_matters: The surviving town marker turns Swego from a broad Huntington reference into a mappable Centerport locality. The listing also shows how a location can be secure even when competing historical interpretations of a name remain unsettled.

rows.title: Sylvester Manor
rows.summary: Sylvester Manor stands on Manchonack / Shelter Island, a Manhansett homeland later transformed into a colonial provisioning plantation tied to Barbados commerce, enslavement, indenture, and Indigenous dispossession. In 1829, Montaukett brothers William and Isaac Pharoah, ages eight and five, were indentured there until age twenty-one. William escaped in 1840 and joined a New London whaling voyage; Isaac completed his indenture and remained at the Manor.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: William and Isaac Pharoah place Montaukett childhood, labor, resistance, maritime skill, and continuity at the center of Sylvester Manor's history. Their lives belong beside the histories of Manhansett homeland, enslaved African labor, Barbados commerce, and colonial dispossession that shaped the Manor landscape.

rows.title: Syosset
rows.summary: Syosset is a documented village name in Oyster Bay, but the available historical interpretation derives it through the Dutch word schout rather than from a Native landscape term.
rows.address_label: Syosset, Town of Oyster Bay, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Not every Long Island name that sounds Indigenous has a confirmed Indigenous origin. Syosset provides a visible correction and demonstrates why language claims should be checked against records instead of repeated from appearance alone.

rows.title: Tackan
rows.summary: Tackan is recorded as a tract of land in Smithtown on the Nissequogue River.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Tatamuckatakis (Great Neck Creek)
rows.summary: Tatamuckatakis is recorded as a neck and creek in Babylon, west of Copiague Neck, now known as Great Neck and Great Neck Creek.

rows.title: Tatamuckatakis / Yatamuntitahege
rows.summary: Yatamuntitahege is treated as a cross-reference to Tatamuckatakis. The related name is tied to a river bounding Copiag Neck in the western part of Babylon.

rows.title: Taukoms (Lacten's Neck)
rows.summary: A Babylon neck placename that preserves Native and English naming layers in the same landscape.

rows.title: Tenkenas (Ward's Island)
rows.summary: Tenkenas was the Native name recorded for Ward's Island in the East River, formerly also called Great Barcut or Great Barn Island.

rows.title: Tersarge / Crab Meadow
rows.summary: Tersarge is a seventeenth-century locality on Long Island's north shore. Later historical research connects the name with the Crab Meadow landscape east of Huntington.
rows.address_label: Crab Meadow Wetlands and Beach, Northport, NY (general area)
rows.why_this_matters: Tersarge ties a surviving Native place name to a documented claim of kinship and inheritance on the north shore. Placing it broadly at Crab Meadow makes the history visible while avoiding a false claim that the seventeenth-century allotment boundary has been precisely reconstructed.

rows.title: The Point
rows.summary: The Point is a Shinnecock Reservation marshland remembered through community use for fishing, hunting, gathering, and teaching across generations. The listing speaks from local Shinnecock landscape knowledge and does not direct readers to sensitive areas.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: The Watermill Center
rows.summary: The Watermill Center is an arts residency, archive, and research library on Shinnecock ancestral territory. Jeremy Dennis developed On This Site there during a June 2017 residency, and Watermill has worked with Shinnecock artists, cultural workers, and staff including Shane Weeks, Andrina Smith, Denise Silva-Dennis, and Kelly Dennis.
rows.address_label: 39 Water Mill Towd Road, Water Mill, NY 11976
rows.listing_image_alt: On This Site, Edition 2, displayed in The Watermill Center research library
rows.ancestral_territory_note: The Watermill Center identifies its ten-acre campus as Shinnecock ancestral territory.
rows.why_this_matters: The Watermill Center connects On This Site's digital map to the residency where its book and exhibition took shape. It also documents sustained Shinnecock artistic labor, administration, education, and collaboration at an institution that identifies its campus as Shinnecock ancestral territory.

rows.title: Tianna / Tiana Bay and Creek
rows.summary: Tianna is a bay and creek name at Good Ground, now Hampton Bays, in western Southampton.

rows.title: Tinnie's Water Hole / Napeague Beach
rows.summary: Tooker recorded Tinnie's as a water hole on Napeague Beach near the Amagansett Hills. The historic water hole has not been matched to a named modern pond, so this marker represents the broader Napeague beach and dune landscape.
rows.address_label: Napeague State Park, East Hampton, NY (broad representative point)
rows.why_this_matters: The name records a small water feature within the Napeague coastal landscape and a story about a woman whose identity was not preserved in the printed account. A broad marker keeps the record searchable without inventing an exact pond or treating an unverified story as established fact.

rows.title: Towapionke (John Wood's Neck)
rows.summary: Towapionke is a tract east of Mastic Neck in Brookhaven, later known as John Wood's Neck.

rows.title: Towd (North Sea Wading Place)
rows.summary: Towd is a locality near North Sea in Southampton, described as a cove above a wading place.

rows.title: Toyonge (Red Creek)
rows.summary: Toyonge is Red Creek at the head of Peconic Bay in Southampton.

rows.title: Tuckahoe (Southampton)
rows.summary: Tuckahoe is a level tract of land and school district north of Southampton Village.

rows.title: Tuckahoe Gate Hill / Shinnecock Hills
rows.summary: Tuckahoe Gate Hill is Tooker's reference to one hill in the Shinnecock Hills range near the historic Tuckahoe gate. The marker represents the broader documented hill landscape rather than claiming an exact summit.
rows.address_label: General Tuckahoe Road / Shinnecock Hills area, Southampton, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: A broad marker keeps this recorded Shinnecock Hills place visible without assigning Tooker's historical label to a private parcel or pretending that the precise hill has been recovered.

rows.title: Turkom (Menantic Neck)
rows.summary: Turkom is a small point or neck between two creeks near Menantic Neck on Shelter Island.

rows.title: Uncawamuck (Reeve's Creek)
rows.summary: Uncawamuck is a creek placename near Mattituck, associated with a canoe portage and the Ocquebauck land-title landscape.

rows.title: Unkawa Neck / Unqua Creek
rows.summary: Unkawa was a neck-place name on the Babylon and Oyster Bay town boundary, connected with the later Unqua stream name.

rows.title: Unkechaug Ancestral Land
rows.summary: A living Unkechaug homeland where reservation history, wetlands, waterways, village landscapes, and legal pressure remain connected.
rows.why_this_matters: Unkechaug Ancestral Land connects Poospatuck and the south shore Brookhaven landscape with a living Native homeland. Land, water, language, governance, and community continuity run from early records to the present.

rows.title: Unkechaug Indian Reservation
rows.summary: The Unkechaug Indian Nation is a Native nation recognized by New York State and centered on the Poospatuck Reservation along Poospatuck Creek in Mastic. The reservation is a continuing homeland where Unkechaug people maintain government, community, language work, and relationships with land and water.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Poospatuck is a living Unkechaug homeland and seat of government, not a remnant of a disappeared people. Its history connects land defense, state law, family continuity, language revitalization, and present-day Native sovereignty on Long Island.

rows.title: Wading River Site
rows.summary: The Wading River Site is the oldest clearly-dated archaic period village site located near the mouth of the Wading River, an ideal place to draw food resources from the freshwater stream and Long Island sound. It's sheltered location protected the villagers from the cold north and western winds, signifying its use in the winter, while abundant shellfish remains show spring and summer occupation; thus the site was used year-round. This camp, according to Ritchie who studied the site in 1955-56, was part of a.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wagaspor (Flatlands Meadows)
rows.summary: Wagaspor is a creek in the Flatlands meadows of Kings County.

rows.title: Wallage / Old Westbury
rows.summary: Wallage is a historical name associated with the Westbury settlement in North Hempstead. Later place histories consistently connect the older locality with the area now known as Old Westbury.
rows.address_label: Old Westbury, Nassau County, NY (representative point)
rows.why_this_matters: Wallage preserves an older layer beneath the names Woodedge, Westbury, and Old Westbury. Mapping the name broadly makes that sequence visible while acknowledging the disagreement in older printed sources.

rows.title: Wampmissic
rows.summary: Wampmissic is a tract of land and large swamp in Brookhaven, between Yaphank and Manor stations on the Long Island Rail Road. The name is interpreted as a place of chestnut trees.

rows.title: Wamponamon (Montauk Point)
rows.summary: Wamponamon is the extreme eastern end of Long Island at Montauk Point, where the lighthouse stands.

rows.title: Wanasquattan (Amityville)
rows.summary: A western Babylon placename near Amityville connected with Massapequa proprietors and a 1696 Huntington grant.

rows.title: Wandowenock (Newtown)
rows.summary: Wandowenock was reported as a name for the eastern portion of Newtown in Queens, with meaning unresolved.

rows.title: Wantagh
rows.summary: Wantagh is connected to recorded forms related to Wiandance or Wyandanch, the Montaukett grand sachem whose name appears widely in Long Island Native history. The modern village adopted Wantagh as a public place name in 1891.
rows.address_label: Wantagh village area
