rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land because Wantagh sits in the south shore region connected with Merrick, Massapequa, and neighboring Native histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Wantagh shows how Native names continue to shape public geography, even when modern usage is separated from the original communities, languages, and political histories. A familiar place name can remember Native presence while leaving important histories unexplained.

rows.title: Warrasketuck Creek
rows.summary: Warrasketuck is a creek at Amityville on the boundary between South Oyster Bay and Babylon. The name is interpreted as the ending or point creek.

rows.title: Warratta Neck
rows.summary: Warratta is a neck of land at Center Moriches between Barnes mill-pond on Terrell River and Senex Creek.

rows.title: Watchogue
rows.summary: An East Moriches neck placename, with a related Islip use west of Bay Shore.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wattuquasset (Lake Montauk)
rows.summary: Wattuquasset is a small neck on the southwest side of Great Pond at Montauk, now Lake Montauk.

rows.title: Waubheag (Rockaway Neck)
rows.summary: Waubheag preserves a Rockaway Neck waterway name in Queens. The name belongs to broad place-name and boundary-record context within the Rockaway and Jamaica Bay landscape.

rows.title: Wauwepex (Cold Spring Harbor)
rows.summary: Wauwepex is the reported Native name for the original settlement on the west side of Cold Spring Harbor. The name is interpreted as a good little water-place.

rows.title: Weckatuck (Neck and Spring)
rows.summary: Weckatuck is a neck and spring placename near the foot of Long Beach by Noyack Road, associated with a nearby Native village and shell-heap site.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Weekewackmamish (Mill Creek)
rows.summary: Weekewackmamish is Mill Creek at Southport in Southampton, emptying into Peconic Bay.

rows.title: Weesuck
rows.summary: Weesuck is the clearer modern form of the longer placename Achabachawesuck. It refers to a small creek or brook between Fourth Neck and Pine Neck in what was historically Atlanticville, now the East Quogue area of Southampton.
rows.address_label: General Weesuck Creek / East Quogue area, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Wegwagonock
rows.summary: Wegwagonock was once a large settlement in what is now the northern shore of Sag Harbor town. In around 1846, the ground containing burials and evidence of a Native village site were destroyed and used as stability material for the ship and oil yards.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Werpos
rows.summary: A Brooklyn placename near Merechkawikingh, recorded in a 1640 Kieft patent and interpreted as a bushy place or thicket.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge
rows.summary: Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge protects habitat along the Carmans River in Shirley and houses the Long Island National Wildlife Refuge Complex visitor center. Inside, an interpretive section shares Unkechaug Nation history and displays objects connected with that history. At the center's November 2011 dedication, representatives of the Unkechaug and Shinnecock Nations offered a traditional blessing, recognizing enduring Native relationships with the river, wetlands, and wildlife.
rows.why_this_matters: Wertheim is not only a protected river and wetland landscape. Its visitor center makes Unkechaug Nation history visible to the public, while the 2011 blessing by Unkechaug and Shinnecock representatives recognized continuing Native relationships with the Carmans River, wetlands, and wildlife.

rows.title: West Woods
rows.summary: West Woods is a forty acre beach and woodland area owned by the Shinnecock Tribe. The woodland and beach area is used for contemporary social gatherings, weddings, celebrations, camping, and sweat lodge ceremonies. In recent times, West Woods has been encroached upon with it's blurred boundaries. At the start of the 1747 100-year timber lease to the Shinnecock by Southampton Town, the land encompassed one hundred acres.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: West Woods Sweat Lodge
rows.summary: West Woods is a contemporary Shinnecock ceremonial landscape. Its public description stays broad to respect community privacy and ceremonial knowledge.
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock ceremonial life continues in living community spaces, not only in historic records. Late twentieth-century accounts document the return and continuation of Shinnecock sweat-lodge ceremonies, including the role of Shinnecock community members and relatives from connected Native communities. References: John A. Strong, "We Are Still Here": The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today (Shinnecock sweat-lodge discussion).

rows.title: Whale's Fin
rows.summary: Whale's Fin is a Shinnecock sacred and cultural place near Shinnecock Inlet, remembered in oral history through whaling, whales coming ashore, and the changing barrier-beach landscape.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Inlet shoreline area, Southampton (generalized)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Whale's Fin connects Shinnecock maritime knowledge with a living cultural landscape. It carries histories of whaling skill, coastal change, and continuing relationships among Shinnecock people, whales, the bay, and the ocean.

rows.title: Whaling
rows.summary: Whaling history on Native Long Island connects whales as living relations, drift-whale harvests, seventeenth-century shore-whaling labor, Shinnecock, Montaukett, and Unkechaug maritime skill, industrial whaling, ecological loss, and present-day whale conservation.
rows.why_this_matters: Whaling history shows Native Long Island as a maritime homeland shaped by reciprocal relationships with whales, skilled Native labor, colonial exploitation, global travel, and present-day responsibility to living whale populations.

rows.title: Wickapogue (Meacox Bay)
rows.summary: Wickapogue is a farming district at the western end of Meacox Bay in Southampton. The name is interpreted as at the end of the pond or water-place.

rows.title: Wickaposset (Fishers Island)
rows.summary: A small eastern-island place name whose variants preserve older coastal geography beyond the main body of Long Island.

rows.title: Wigwagonock (Sag Harbor)
rows.summary: Wigwagonock is a Sag Harbor placename associated with land east of Division Street and an Indigenous village site near Sleight's Hill.

rows.title: Wigwame Swamp (Cold Spring Harbor)
rows.summary: Wigwame, or Wigwam, is recorded as a swamp in Huntington town. A local note places the early "wigwam swamp" where the main part of Cold Spring Harbor village now stands.

rows.title: William Floyd Estate
rows.summary: In exchange for reconfirming previous land deeds between the Unkechaug and colonist Colonel William Tangier Smith, Smith granted in perpetuity one hundred and seventy-five acres of land to the tribe on Mastic Neck. The grant stated that the Unkechaug, " their children and the posterity of their children forever shall without molestation from me or my heirs or assigns shall and may plant and sowe forever " and added that the Indians could not sell, convey, or alienate this planting right or any part thereof to any.
rows.address_label: 245 Park Dr, Mastic Beach, NY 11951
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winganhauppauge
rows.summary: An Islip brook-and-neck placename sometimes associated with Champlain's Creek, preserving a waterway name before later English naming.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winganhauppauge (Champlain's Creek)
rows.summary: Winganhauppauge is an Islip placename tied to a neck of land and brook also associated with Champlain's Creek.

rows.title: Winippague
rows.summary: Winippague is the traditional placename for what is now Bergen Island in Jamaica Bay. The alternative name is Wimbaccoe. Anthropologist William Wallace Tooker suggested that the name may translate to "a fine water-place," from wini, "fine," and -paug, "water-place." Winippague or Bergen Island has been identified as an important wampum manufacturing place for Canarsie people during early contact with Europeans. Archaeological materials from the area are held in Smithsonian collections.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winippague (Bergen Island)
rows.summary: Winippague is recorded for Bergen Island in Jamaica Bay, with Wimbaccoe linked as a related form.

rows.title: Winne-comack / Commack
rows.summary: Winne-comack is associated with modern Commack. Shorter Comac and Comack forms are kept as alternate spellings of the same placename rather than separate map sites.

rows.title: Winnecomac / Commack
rows.summary: Winnecomac is the older placename behind Commack, a hamlet spanning Huntington and Smithtown.

rows.title: Winnecroscoms Neck (Mastic)
rows.summary: Winnecroscoms is a neck of land in Brookhaven town, one of the necks into which Mastic was divided. Related forms include Winocrosscombs, Wenacroscoms, Wenicroscoms, Winecroscum, and Wannuggeashcum.

rows.title: Wisquosucks (Squassucks Point)
rows.summary: Wisquosucks is a Brookhaven placename for Squassucks Point on the Carmans River, associated with an Unkechaug person recorded in deeds and leases.

rows.title: Wonunke (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Wonunke is a Westhampton placename for necks of land east of Beaver Dam River, later appearing in Great and Little Wonunk forms.

rows.title: Wooruskhouse (Probable Copiague Neck)
rows.summary: Rev. Azariah Horton repeatedly mentioned Wooruskhouse in 1741-1743 and located it about three miles from West Neck. The distance, his south-shore travel, the Town of Babylon's historic neck sequence, and the name's possible reference to a point of land make Copiague Neck the strongest modern inference, but not a proven identification.
rows.address_label: Copiague Neck, Town of Babylon, NY (probable broad identification)
rows.why_this_matters: Wooruskhouse records an eighteenth-century Native community landscape along Babylon's south shore. A probable marker restores that name to the map while making the limits of the surviving evidence visible instead of turning Horton's distance note into false certainty.

rows.title: Wopowog (Stony Brook)
rows.summary: Wopowog is recorded for Stony Brook in Brookhaven town, with Wopawog appearing in earlier Long Island history writing.

rows.title: Wuchebehsuck (Montauk North Neck)
rows.summary: A Montauk North Neck valley name associated with a small pond outlet and the 1670 Montauk deed.

rows.title: Wyamaug / Miamogue (Simmons Point)
rows.summary: Wyamaug, also recorded as Miamogue, Miamegg, and Miamuck, is a Jamesport placename associated with Simmons Point.

rows.title: Wyandance / Wyandanch
rows.summary: Wyandance, now Wyandanch, is a Babylon placename preserving the name of the seventeenth-century sachem of Paumanack.

rows.title: Yaphank / Yamphanke
rows.summary: Yaphank is a Brookhaven village name originally applied to a creek south of the hamlet. Yamphanke is an earlier recorded form.

rows.title: Yaphank, Weeks Pond Settlement
rows.summary: Yaphank, a village in Brookhaven town, was originally the name of the creek south of the hamlet. A land deed signed in 1664 by Unkechaug Sachem Tobacus mentions a river called Yamphanke. In the 17th century, the Unkechaug Indians, who had their primary residence in nearby Mastic, built temporary campsites near what was later known as Weeks Pond.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Yennecock / Southold Town
rows.summary: Yennicock, now known as Southold Town, was once land occupied by the Corchaugs people who inhabited the North Fork of eastern Long Island. The land was deeded in 1665.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Yennicock / Yennicott (Southold)
rows.summary: Yennicock is recorded as the supposed Indigenous name of the locality where Southold village stands. Related sources use Yennicott for the wider North Fork area.

rows.title: Yonáhqôsunuk
rows.summary: The Smith Site near Smith Cove preserves evidence of Indigenous use across more than one season as well as an ancestral resting place. Public descriptions remain broad to protect ancestors, cultural belongings, and archaeological deposits.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Smith Cove landscape records enduring Indigenous use of Shelter Island across seasons. It also shows why older archaeological reports must be read critically: ancestors and burial belongings are not objects of curiosity, and precise burial information requires protection.
